Assuming DM only interacts with electrons, and taking the target system to be at zero temperature, the relevant dynamic structure factor is

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≡2​πV​∑f|⟨f|∑kei​𝐪⋅𝐫k|i⟩|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{f}|\langle f|\sum_{k}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{k}}|i\rangle|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega) (53)

where kk sums over all electrons and the initial and final states are generic many-body states. The first calculations of DM-electron scattering assumed that |i⟩,|f⟩|i\rangle,|f\rangle are single-excitation Bloch states and that the sum over all electrons could be replaced by the operator ei​𝐪⋅𝐫e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}} acting only on a single electron; however, as commented on at the beginning of this section, for low q<qcohq<q_{\rm coh} it is not clearly justified to assume that only interactions with a single electron dominate. Related to that, it is also not obvious that only Fock states are relevant and electron-electron interactions can be neglected. Indeed, while an important step forward, this single particle approach turns out to miss some important many-body effects.

A more general approach can be taken, where we do not make any assumptions about the many-body states. The discussion here is largely based off of Refs. [79, 80, 81]. We instead rewrite the dynamic structure factor in terms of the electron number density operator,

n𝐪=∑kei​𝐪⋅𝐫k=∫d3​𝐫​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫​∑k=1Nδ(3)​(𝐫−𝐫k)n_{\mathbf{q}}=\sum_{k}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{k}}=\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{k}) (54)

and focus on understanding the quantity

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≡2​πV​∑f|⟨f|n𝐪|i⟩|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ω).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{f}|\langle f|n_{\mathbf{q}}|i\rangle|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega). (55)

The structure factor is related to the rate to produce charge excitations in the medium, which can be rewritten in terms of the imaginary part of a correlation function:

S(𝐪,ω)=−2Im(−iV∫0∞dtei​ω​t⟨[n𝐪(t),n−𝐪(0)]⟩).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=-2\,{\rm Im}\left(-\frac{i}{V}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle\left[n_{\mathbf{q}}(t),n_{-\mathbf{q}}(0)\right]\rangle\right). (56)

This is a special case of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem (which is slightly more general, applying to finite-temperature systems as well), but can be understood simply as a consequence of unitarity or an application of the optical theorem. This correlation function determines the linear response of the charge density in a medium to any external perturbation, whether it is dark matter or a SM probe. Indeed, consider subjecting the material to some other external potential Φext\Phi_{\rm ext} which also couples linearly to electron density. A suitable candidate is an electromagnetic potential, and we can think of the potential as being sourced by a weak external charge ρext​(𝐪,ω)\rho_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{q},\omega), with Φext=4​π​ρext​(𝐪,ω)/q2\Phi_{\rm ext}=4\pi\rho_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{q},\omega)/q^{2}. Gauss’s law in a medium tells us the response of the electric fields in Fourier space:

i​𝐪⋅𝐄⁡(𝐪,ω)=ρext​(𝐪,ω)ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)i\mathbf{q}\cdot{\bf E}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{\rho_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{q},\omega)}{\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)} (57)

where 𝐄⁡(𝐪,ω){\bf E}(\mathbf{q},\omega) is the total field in the medium and the right hand side of the equation is the total charge density. The total charge density is the sum of the external charge density and the induced charge density in the medium, and is related to the external charge density by 1/ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)1/\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega). The fact that ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)≠1\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)\neq 1 generically is a manifestation of charge screening, since the external field is scaled down by ϵ\epsilon to generate the in-medium field which a test charge in the material would feel. Meanwhile, because the induced charge density is due to the response of the medium, it is determined by the correlation function appearing in Eq. (56). This gives a relationship between S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) and the dielectric response [82]:

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=q22​π​α​Im​(−1ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)),S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{q^{2}}{2\pi\alpha}{\rm Im}\left(-\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)}\right), (58)

which will be investigated in much more detail in Sec. V.3. Note that we have made the approximation of a homogeneous medium, and ignored some subtleties here regarding the fact that we are in a periodic medium. We also implicitly work with the longitudinal dielectric function everywhere here, since only the longitudinal fields appear in Gauss’s law.

The advantage of this point of view is that we have made no assumptions about the nature of the exact eigenstates |f⟩|f\rangle of the target. At this point, however, we must find some way to calculate or determine ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega). We first proceed by close analogy to the calculation of the photon polarization in field theory. The dielectric function ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega) is by definition related to the longitudinal photon polarization ΠL\Pi_{L}, with the exact relationship given by ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)=1−ΠL​(𝐪,ω)/|𝐪|2\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)=1-\Pi_{L}(\mathbf{q},\omega)/|\mathbf{q}|^{2}. This suggests an approach to calculating the polarization in terms of single-particle Bloch states as derived above. In Sec. V.3, we will describe a number of analytic models for the dynamic structure factor, as well as explicit numerical calculations using Bloch wavefunctions. The result from including the full many-body states (or equivalently of including screening in the single-particle picture) leads to matrix elements with qualitatively different behavior.

For example, in generic solid-state systems (including both semiconductors like silicon and metals like aluminum), there is a resonance for q≲pFq\lesssim p_{F} called the plasmon, which appears in the dynamic structure factor as

S⁡(𝐪,ω)∝q2​ω​ωp2​Γp(ωp2−ω2)2+ω2​Γp2.S(\mathbf{q},\omega)\propto q^{2}\omega\frac{\omega_{p}^{2}\Gamma_{p}}{(\omega_{p}^{2}-\omega^{2})^{2}+\omega^{2}\Gamma_{p}^{2}}. (59)

with Γp\Gamma_{p} a finite width which regulates the resonance. The appearance of the plasma frequency

ωp=4​π​α​neme\omega_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi\alpha n_{e}}{m_{e}}} (60)

suggests an interpretation of this resonance as the collective oscillation of the entire valence electron density nen_{e}, which is not visible in a picture of single-particle wavefunctions. The quantized mode corresponding to the collective excitation is also known as a plasmon, where we can interpret this result as this structure factor for producing a single plasmon. Since the ground state is an eigenfunction of the density operator for 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 (with eigenvalue equal to the total number of particles in the system), the factor of q2q^{2} in Eq. (59) can be understood as enforcing that the overlap of the initial ground state and the final state with an excited plasmon should vanish as q→0q\to 0.

We may also express the DM scattering rate directly in terms of the experimentally-measured loss function or energy loss function (ELF),

𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)≡Im⁡(−1ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)),\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv{\rm Im}\left(-\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)}\right), (61)

without ever using explicit electron wavefunctions. (This also only applies as long as the DM-electron interactions are spin-independent and couple to electron density.) Indeed, the same loss function describes energy loss of electrons in materials and X-ray scattering, providing a way to determine the loss function from experimental data in a way that automatically accounts for all many-body and screening effects. These measurements are exactly analogous to how deep inelastic scattering experiments can probe the degrees of freedom in the proton, in particular the non-perturbative proton form factors at low momentum transfer, by exploiting the electron coupling to quarks. Fig. 3 shows the measured ELF in silicon with a clear plasmon resonance. One can also use phenomenological models of the dielectric function satisfying various properties with parameters fit to the data; for instance, this is done with the Mermin oscillator model fit to optical data or electron energy loss [84, 85, 86], as well we also discuss in Sec. V.3. The disadvantage of the latter approaches is that the connection to individual quantized excitations, like the number of electron/hole pairs produced in a given scattering event, is less transparent. In addition, it can be difficult to experimentally determine some regimes in energy and momentum transfer that are relevant for DM scattering.

III.2.2 Phonons

The dynamic structure factor for nuclear scattering is given by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≡2​πV​∑f|⟨f|∑IfI​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫I|i⟩|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{f}|\langle f|\sum_{I}f_{I}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{I}}|i\rangle|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega) (62)

where fIf_{I} are again the normalized interaction strengths with the ions. The relative scattering strength will depend on the type of ion, and the factors fIf_{I} do not factorize out of the structure factor if the system is composed of different types of ions. Thus, in contrast to the electron-excitation dynamic structure factor, for multi-atom target materials there is not a single dynamic structure, but a continuous class of structure factors depending on how the external probe couples to the individual atoms. As will be discussed further later, this allows for additional interesting effects in the material-dependence of DM scattering, as a way to distinguish different DM coupling scenarios. Note that in this work we will restrict to spin-independent DM interaction strengths fIf_{I}; if there is a spin-dependent interaction potential, then one must also perform an average over all possible spin states of the ions. An extensive review of the dynamic structure factor for phonons, including such spin-dependent interactions, can be found in Ref. [87].

For phonon excitations, the final states can simply be written by acting with the phonon creation operators introduced in Eq. (49) on the vacuum. For a single phonon being created, |f⟩=aν,𝐤†​|0⟩|f\rangle=a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}|0\rangle, while multiphonon excitations are also possible. In order to detect the phonon excitations being created, the energy deposited is necessarily well above the operating temperature of the experiment, and it is a good approximation to take T=0T=0 and assume |i⟩=|0⟩|i\rangle=|0\rangle for the initial state. In order to compute the matrix elements with these states, we must write the ion positions as 𝐫I=𝐫n​j+𝐮n​j\mathbf{r}_{I}=\mathbf{r}_{nj}+\mathbf{u}_{nj}, where 𝐫n​j=𝐑n+𝐑j0\mathbf{r}_{nj}=\mathbf{R}_{n}+\mathbf{R}^{0}_{j} is the equilibrium position of the ion jj in the unit cell labeled by nn and the ion displacement 𝐮n​j\mathbf{u}_{nj} contains the phonon creation and annihilation operators. Substituting this into the exponential appearing in the matrix element gives:

fIei​𝐪⋅𝐫I=fjei​𝐪⋅𝐫n​jexp(i𝐪⋅∑ν,𝐤12​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤[aν,𝐤†𝐞ν,𝐤,j∗e−i𝐤⋅𝐫n​j+aν,𝐤𝐞ν,𝐤,jei​𝐤⋅𝐫n​j]).f_{I}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{I}}=f_{j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}\exp\left(i\mathbf{q}\cdot\sum_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}}\left[a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}+a_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{e}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}\right]\right). (63)

Expanding this operator will contain a 0-phonon contribution, a 1-phonon creation contribution, and so on. (Note that in Eq. (49) we gave the time-dependent Heisenberg or interaction picture operator 𝐮n,j​(t)\mathbf{u}_{n,j}(t), but the matrix elements given in Eq. (62) are computed with the Schrödinger operators where the time-dependence of the states has already been taken into account in Fermi’s Golden rule, leading to the energy-conserving delta function. This is why the time-dependent phase factors have been removed in substituting in Eq. (49).)

To perform the expansion explicitly in terms of phonon creation and annihilation operators, we can make use of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula for generic operators AA and BB:

exp⁡(A)​exp⁡(B)=exp⁡(A+B+12​[A,B]+112​[A,[A,B]]−112​[B,[A,B]]​…),\exp(A)\exp(B)=\exp\left(A+B+\frac{1}{2}[A,B]+\frac{1}{12}[A,[A,B]]-\frac{1}{12}[B,[A,B]]\dots\right)~, (64)

which simplifies in the case of the harmonic oscillator algebra because the first commutator [a,a†]=1[a,a^{\dagger}]=1 is a cc-number and truncates the series at the third term. Applying this gives

fI​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫I=fj​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫n​j​e−Wj​(𝐪)​∏ν,𝐤exp⁡(i𝐪⋅𝐞∗ν,𝐤,je−i𝐤⋅𝐫n​j2​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤​aν,𝐤†)​exp⁡(i​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐤,j​ei​𝐤⋅𝐫n​j2​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤​aν,𝐤),\displaystyle f_{I}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{I}}=f_{j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\prod_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\exp\left(\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}}{\sqrt{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}}a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\right)\exp\left(\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}}{\sqrt{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}}a_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\right), (65)

with

Wj​(𝐪)≡12​∑ν,𝐤|𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐤,j∗|22​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤.W_{j}(\mathbf{q})\equiv\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\frac{|\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}|^{2}}{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}. (66)

The factor e−Wj​(𝐪)e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})} is also known as the Debye-Waller factor, which roughly speaking accounts for the effect of the zero-point motion of the ions in the lattice. Taking the matrix element with the initial vacuum state, the exponential of the phonon annihilation operators reduces to unity and we can write the structure factor as

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=2​πV​∑f|⟨f|∑n,jfj​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫n​j​e−Wj​(𝐪)​∏ν,𝐤exp⁡(i𝐪⋅𝐞∗ν,𝐤,je−i𝐤⋅𝐫n​j2​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤​aν,𝐤†)|0⟩|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ω).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{f}\left|\langle f|\sum_{n,j}f_{j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\prod_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\exp\left(\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}}{\sqrt{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}}a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\right)|0\rangle\right|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega). (67)

where we have replaced the sum over II with a sum over n,jn,j.

Taking only the zeroth-order term in the exponential of phonon creation operators aν,𝐤†a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}, there are no phonon transitions, and this just corresponds to DM elastically recoiling off the lattice as a whole. The leading nontrivial contribution comes from expanding the exponentials to linear order, which allows for single-phonon creation. Summing over final states |f⟩=aν,𝐤†​|0⟩|f\rangle=a^{\dagger}_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}|0\rangle, this leads to the single-phonon structure factor

S(1−p​h)​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle S^{(1-ph)}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =2​πV​∑ν,𝐤|∑n,jfj​ei⁡(𝐪−𝐤)⋅𝐫n​j​e−Wj​(𝐪)​i​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐤,j∗2​Ncell​Mj​ων,𝐤|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ων,𝐤)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}\left|\sum_{n,j}f_{j}e^{i(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{r}_{nj}}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{k},j}}{\sqrt{2N_{\rm cell}M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}}}\right|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{k}}) (68)

We next use the fact that for 𝐪\mathbf{q} smaller than any reciprocal lattice vector 𝐆\mathbf{G}, the sum over lattice sites simply enforces momentum conservation:99 9 Since reciprocal lattice vectors are defined by the condition ei​𝐆⋅𝐑=1e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{R}}=1, momentum is only conserved up to a reciprocal lattice vector, 𝐤=𝐪+𝐆\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{G}. For nonzero 𝐆\mathbf{G}, this is called Umklapp scattering.

∑nei⁡(𝐪−𝐤)⋅𝐑n=Ncell​δ𝐪,𝐤\sum_{n}e^{i(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k})\cdot\mathbf{R}_{n}}=N_{\rm cell}\delta_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}} (69)

since phonon modes are only defined for 𝐤\mathbf{k} within 1BZ. This implies that we will have excitation of any phonon with the same momentum 𝐪\mathbf{q} and energy ω\omega. The single-phonon structure factor then simplifies to

S(1−p​h)​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle S^{(1-ph)}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =2​π​NcellV​∑ν|∑jfj​e−Wj​(𝐪)​i​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗2​Mj​ων,𝐪|2​δ​(Ef−Ei−ων,𝐪)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi N_{\rm cell}}{V}\sum_{\nu}\left|\sum_{j}f_{j}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}}{\sqrt{2M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}}}\right|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}})
≡2​πΩ​∑ν|Fν​(𝐪)|2ων,𝐪​δ​(Ef−Ei−ων,𝐪)\displaystyle\equiv\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\sum_{\nu}\frac{|F_{\nu}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}}{\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}}\delta(E_{f}-E_{i}-\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}) (70)

where the second line defines a single-phonon form factor Fν​(𝐪)F_{\nu}(\mathbf{q}) and we defined Ω=V/Ncell\Omega=V/N_{\rm cell} as the primitive unit cell volume. This form factor sums over the coupling of the probe with the ions fjf_{j} in the unit cell, multiplied by the normalized motion of that ion ∝𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗/Mj\propto\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}/\sqrt{M_{j}} and is therefore describing an effective coupling of the probe with a particular phonon mode, accounting for interference effects. This structure factor therefore describes coherent scattering off the ions in the lattice. However, we explicitly see the 1-phonon form factor is an intrinsic quantity of the material and does not scale with the size of the system.

Neglecting the details of this (probe-dependent) form factor, the 1-phonon structure factor has an amplitude that can be estimated as ∼q2/(2​M​ω𝐪,ν)\sim q^{2}/(2M\omega_{\mathbf{q},\nu}), and we see from Eq. (67) that excitations of more phonons will be expected to give a contribution to the structure factor that roughly scales as

|⟨n|∑IfI​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫I|0⟩|2∼(q22​M​ω0)n\left|\langle n|\sum_{I}f_{I}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{I}}|0\rangle\right|^{2}\sim\left(\frac{q^{2}}{2M\omega_{0}}\right)^{n} (71)

for a final state with nn phonons. Here we have replaced MjM_{j} with some averaged ion mass MM, and ω𝐪,ν\omega_{\mathbf{q},\nu} with a typical phonon energy ω0\omega_{0} that will be some average over acoustic and optical phonons, to give a heuristic scaling.1010 10 Of course, to actually obtain the structure factor S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega), these matrix elements must be computed with interference effects and integrated over the phase space such that the phonon energies match ω\omega, which can change the scaling for specific final states and/or couplings. Another subtlety is that the single-phonon piece of the operator ei​𝐪⋅𝐫Ie^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{I}} can also give rise to two (or more phonon) excitations through anharmonic interactions in the phonon Hamiltonian. The next term in the phonon Hamiltonian ∼(𝐮)3\sim(\mathbf{u})^{3}, which comes from expanding the potential to higher order in the displacements. A more detailed discussion of the various contributions to the two-phonon dynamic structure factor can be found in Ref. [88]. This approximate scaling gives an estimate of the importance of higher-order phonon excitations to the structure factor, depending on the regime of momentum transfer qq. Note that for a harmonic oscillator mode with energy ω0\omega_{0}, 2​M​ω0\sqrt{2M\omega_{0}} corresponds to the momentum spread of the ground-state wavefunction of a particle of mass MM in a harmonic oscillator potential with frequency ω\omega. Taking as typical parameters M∼30​mpM\sim 30m_{p} and ω0∼50\omega_{0}\sim 50 meV, the momentum spread is about 50 keV. We can thus interpret the expansion in q2/2​M​ω0q^{2}/2M\omega_{0} as follows: at low qq compared to the momentum spread, the dynamic structure factor will be dominated by the 1-phonon contribution since higher-energy excitations have a suppressed overlap with the probe potential. As qq becomes comparable to 2​M​ω0\sqrt{2M\omega_{0}}, higher order phonon contributions are important, and for q≫2​M​ω0q\gg\sqrt{2M\omega_{0}}, the structure factor will transition to that of free nuclear recoils since the kinetic energy will dominate over potential energy. In Sec. IV below, we will illustrate this more explicitly with simple model of a single ion in a harmonic oscillator, and follow the transitions down from the high-qq regime of incoherent scattering off a single nucleus, to the regime of low-qq coherent scattering which leads to single or few-phonon production.

Finally, we note that the formalism for phonon production through coherent nuclear scattering may apply to systems other than crystal lattices, including superfluid helium which is actively being investigated as a potential experimental target. We will discuss this in Sec. IV.3.

IV Dark Matter-Nucleon Scattering

A microscopic theory of DM interactions with quarks and/or gluons yields an effective coupling of DM to nucleons, which may include neutrons as well as protons. This may be parameterized by a fiducial DM-nucleon cross section, σ¯n\overline{\sigma}_{n}, which by default is assumed to be a spin-independent scattering cross section. Traditional direct detection of WIMP DM has exclusively focused on DM-nuclear scattering by treating the nuclei as free target particles at rest. Here we briefly review the parametrics and the main results to draw a contrast with the phenomenology of sub-GeV DM scattering; a more complete treatment can be found in Ref. [89].

DM heavier than about 10 GeV carries kinetic energy greater than 10 keV, well in excess of any displacement energy, and likewise carries momentum greater than 10 MeV which exceeds any zero-point lattice momenta. Thus the nuclear target may be treated as a free particle, and in particular as a momentum eigenstate, so that classical 2-body scattering kinematics applies. In addition, the nucleus may be treated as being at rest initially. We can then use the kinematic relationship in Eq. (9), setting the energy deposited to ω=ER=q2/(2​mN)\omega=E_{R}=q^{2}/(2m_{N}) for a nucleus NN, which gives the relationship

𝐪⋅𝐯=q22​μχ​N(elastic​nuclear​scattering)\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\frac{q^{2}}{2\mu_{\chi N}}\qquad{\rm(elastic\ nuclear\ scattering)} (72)

where μχ​N\mu_{\chi N} is the DM-nucleus reduced mass. For incoming DM with speed vv, the maximum momentum which may be transferred is qmax=2​μχ​N​vq_{\rm max}=2\mu_{\chi N}v, and so the maximum nuclear recoil energy is

ER,max=qmax22​mN=2​μχ​N2​v2mN.E_{R,\rm max}=\frac{q_{\rm max}^{2}}{2m_{N}}=\frac{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}v^{2}}{m_{N}}. (73)

The best kinematic match is obtained when mχ∼mNm_{\chi}\sim m_{N}, when the free nucleus dispersion relation passes through the region of phase space with q∼mχ​vq\sim m_{\chi}v and ω=q2/(2​mχ)\omega=q^{2}/(2m_{\chi}). For mχ≪mNm_{\chi}\ll m_{N}, as is the case for sub-GeV DM, this energy transfer becomes very inefficient: not only does the incoming DM energy scale as mχm_{\chi}, but only a fraction ∼mχ/mN\sim m_{\chi}/m_{N} is transferred to the nucleus. Indeed, collective modes like phonons can provide a much better kinematic match to the DM. From Eq. (10), the minimum velocity vminv_{\rm min} required to generate a nuclear recoil of energy ERE_{R} is

vmin=mN​ER2​μχ​N2,v_{\rm min}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}}}, (74)

so that a hard upper limit to ERE_{R} is obtained by setting vminv_{\rm min} to the maximum speed of DM in the local neighborhood, assumed to be vesc+v⊕v_{\rm esc}+v_{\oplus} in the Standard Halo Model.

Assuming a contact potential between DM and nucleon, the interaction Hamiltonian is given by

Δ​Hχ​T=π​σ¯nμχ​n2​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫n−𝐫χ),\Delta H_{\chi T}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi\bar{\sigma}_{n}}{\mu^{2}_{\chi n}}}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\ e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{n}-\mathbf{r}_{\chi})}, (75)

where σ¯n\overline{\sigma}_{n} is the DM-nucleon scattering cross section and μχ​n\mu_{\chi n} is the DM-nucleon reduced mass. For simplicity, we assume the same coupling to protons and neutrons. Summing over all available target nuclei NnucN_{\rm nuc}, the dynamic structure factor for elastic nuclear recoils is given by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=2​π​NnucV​A2​|FN​(q)|2​δ​(ω−q22​mN),S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi N_{\rm nuc}}{V}A^{2}|F_{N}(q)|^{2}\,\delta\!\left(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{N}}\right), (76)

where AA is the mass number and FNF_{N} is a nuclear form factor,

FN​(q)=⟨N|1A​∑α=1Aei​𝐪⋅𝐫α|N⟩.F_{N}(q)=\langle N|\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{A}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}}|N\rangle. (77)

Here |N⟩|N\rangle is the bound state of nucleons in a nucleus and α\alpha sums over all nucleons in the nucleus. |FN​(q)|2|F_{N}(q)|^{2} thus captures the strength of response of the system, similar to what we will calculate for a condensed matter target, with the difference that the excited states in a nucleus are usually too high in energy (∼\sim MeV) to be excited by the light DM which is the focus of this review. In what follows, we will always take the initial and final states are both the ground state of the nucleus. |FN​(q)|2|F_{N}(q)|^{2} can be computed in specific nuclear shell models, but for our purposes we can just model it as the Fourier transform of the nucleon mass distribution. FNF_{N} then parameterizes the loss of coherence over all of the nucleons in the nucleus as the momentum transfer becomes comparable to the inverse nuclear radius: this is usually relevant for WIMP DM, but universally irrelevant for sub-GeV DM, so we will always set FN=1F_{N}=1 in what follows.

We can now use the isotropic rate in Eq. (11) to obtain the rate for a target with mass number AA. Performing the trivial ω\omega integral, this gives the nuclear recoil rate:

R=NT​ρχmχ​A2​σ¯n2​μχ​n2​∫q​𝑑q​η​(vmin​(ER))​FN2​(q)R=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{A^{2}\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int q\,dq\,\eta(v_{\rm min}(E_{R}))F^{2}_{N}(q) (78)

where NT=Nnuc/(ρT​V)N_{T}=N_{\rm nuc}/(\rho_{T}V) is the number of target nuclei per unit detector mass. Usually the qq integral can be replaced with q​d​q→d​ER​mNq\,dq\to dE_{R}m_{N} to obtain a differential rate per recoil energy, d​R/d​ERdR/dE_{R}. Apart from η\eta and FNF_{N}, the spectrum is flat in ERE_{R}: all recoil energies are equally likely. The ERE_{R} dependence of the velocity integral is quite important, though: using the Maxwellian ansatz for fχ​(𝐯)f_{\chi}(\mathbf{v}), we have

η⁡(vmin)∝exp⁡(−mN​ER2​μχ​N2​σv2),\eta(v_{\rm min})\propto\exp\left(-\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}\sigma_{v}^{2}}\right), (79)

so in fact the spectrum is exponentially falling in ERE_{R}.

To summarize, the maximum nuclear recoil energy drops as mχ2m_{\chi}^{2} as the DM mass drops below mNm_{N}, while the spectrum is exponentially falling with ERE_{R}. Traditional direct detection of WIMP DM uses heavy target nuclei such as Xe and have thresholds for nuclear recoil detection at ∼\sim few keV, severely limiting sensitivity to GeV-scale DM. Given the exponentially-falling rate, reducing energy thresholds is key to extending sensitivity to lower mass dark matter, and generally results in large increases in rate. For a given detector energy threshold, lighter target nuclei are also preferred for lighter DM, although there are clearly limits to this strategy for sub-GeV DM.

Importantly, this description in terms of free nuclear recoils will start to break down for DM below the GeV scale, since we run into the energy and momentum scales relevant for ions in a condensed matter target. There are several assumptions made in Eq. (78) that will no longer hold. One assumption was that any initial motion of the nucleus in the medium could be neglected, and that we could treat the nucleus wavefunction as a plane wave. However, as qq approaches the typical zero point momentum for an ion in a medium, ∼30−100\sim 30-100 keV in solid state materials, then the bound nature of the nucleus cannot be neglected and we must account for nontrivial ion wavefunctions. In addition, we assumed that the momentum transfer was high enough that only individual nuclear recoils had to be considered. This led to a total elastic recoil rate which was quadratic in A2A^{2}, indicative of coherent scattering off of all the nucleons in a given nucleus, and linear in the total number of target nuclei, indicative of incoherent scattering off of all the nuclei in the target. As qq drops below the scale ≲30\lesssim 30 keV, the DM can probe multiple ions and we must consider final states involving correlated motions of the ions. This will lead to coherent scattering off the medium, or phonon production. Fig. 4 illustrates these different regimes for the nuclear response in q,ωq,\omega as compared with the kinematically allowed region for different sub-GeV DM masses: DM with mχ≳100m_{\chi}\gtrsim 100 MeV will dominantly excite free elastic recoils, DM with 10 MeV ≲mχ≲100\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 100 MeV will probe the bound nature of a nucleus (leading to the multiphonon regime), and DM with mχ≲m_{\chi}\lesssim 10 MeV will mainly excite single phonons. In the rest of the section, we will go through these latter two momentum regimes in detail.

The current limits on DM-nuclear scattering are summarized in Fig. 5 (left). The reach at low masses is driven entirely by the detector thresholds, which are currently at the eV scale for solid-state detectors (see Sec. VII); the curve labeled “Collar 2018” refers to a liquid scintillator detector [93], for which the electron scattering reach is discussed further in Sec. V.2. At higher mass the reach is driven by exposure, which is somewhat limited for the low-threshold prototype detectors which have gram-scale masses. The projections for future kg-year exposure experiments with sub-eV thresholds, sensitive to single phonons produced from a DM-nucleus contact interaction, are summarized in Fig. 5 (right). Searches for DM-nucleus scattering mediated by a dark photon require a more careful choice of target material, and are discussed in Sec. IV.2.1, with reach projections summarized in Fig. 7.

IV.1 From nucleons to phonons: a harmonic oscillator model

As the DM mass drops below ∼\sim GeV, the free-nucleus recoil energy ∼(mχ​v)2/mN\sim(m_{\chi}v)^{2}/m_{N} becomes comparable to the typical energy to break a molecular bond or displace an ion in a crystal, 𝒪⁡(10)\mathcal{O}(10) eV. Indeed, a possible direct detection signature of sub-GeV might be chemical bond breaking or production of defects in crystals [94, 95]. However, for MeV-scale DM and below, nuclear scattering might not have enough energy to displace a nucleus or break a bond, and we must then consider the relevant eigenstates and energies of the bound nucleus. For a crystal, this can become complicated since the nuclei (ions) are all coupled, which leads to the phonon excitations at low energies. However, if we restrict to the DM mass range above 𝒪⁡(10)\mathcal{O}(10) MeV, then the typical momentum transfer q∼mχ​v≳𝒪⁡(10)q\sim m_{\chi}v\gtrsim\mathcal{O}(10) keV. Then it is still possible to take an incoherent approximation where we can model DM scattering as occurring off of an individual bound nucleus in the crystal, as long as the deposited energy remains below the displacement energy.

Thus, in the DM mass range of tens of MeV up to 1 GeV, a useful toy model for DM-nucleon scattering is provided by considering a single nucleus subject to a simple harmonic oscillator potential sourced by its neighboring ions. The toy model allows us to explicitly see the transition from free nuclear recoils to single or few-phonon transitions in crystals, and gives some additional intuition for the phonon dynamic structure factor discussed in Sec. III.2.2 without the complicated details of the phonon band structure and eigenstates. The toy model can also be used to describe a simple system of a diatomic molecule, as an intermediary system between free atoms and condensed matter systems, in the limit of small anharmonic corrections to the potential. In this section, we will give a description of the potential DM signal that comes from exciting bound states of a harmonic potential, as a prelude to single or few-phonon excitations in condensed matter systems.1111 11 For an interesting and detailed study on the possibility of detecting molecular excitations induced by DM scattering in a gaseous target, see Ref. [96].

The harmonic potential we will work with is given by

𝒱⁡(r)=12​mN​ω02​r2,\mathcal{V}(r)=\frac{1}{2}m_{N}\omega_{0}^{2}r^{2}, (80)

where we can interpret the harmonic oscillator level nn as an nn-phonon state in a crystal (where rr is the displacement from the equilibrium position), or a bound state in molecule (where rr is the interatomic distance). For a diatomic molecular system, the mass mNm_{N} should be replaced by the reduced mass of the system. To solidify the interpretation of nn-phonon states in a crystal, note that if we take ω0=60​meV\omega_{0}=60\ {\rm meV}, a typical phonon energy for silicon, and r0=0.235​nmr_{0}=0.235\ {\rm nm} equal to the nearest-neighbor distance in a Si lattice, we obtain 𝒱⁡(r0)=66​eV\mathcal{V}(r_{0})=66\ {\rm eV}, on the same order as the maximum displacement energy of 47 eV along the [110] direction [97]. The motivation for using ω0=60​meV\omega_{0}=60\ {\rm meV} is that if a single nucleus is struck with a large momentum transfer, the motion will have a large overlap with the phonon modes at the edges of the 1BZ, where the ions have more random motions and energies ∼60\sim 60 meV.

We will again assume a contact interaction as in Eq. (75) for simplicity, with equal proton and neutron couplings. Because we are still in the incoherent regime, the form of the rate will be very similar to that of Eq. (78), except that we must use the bound states of the nucleus for the target-dependent form factors. In this regime, the momentum transfer is too low to probe the nuclear structure, so the nuclear form factor in Eq. (77) can be taken to be unity and is not relevant for this discussion. The rate in this model is given by

R=NT​ρχmχ​A2​σ¯n2​μχ​n2​∫q​𝑑q​∑n|f⁡(n,𝐪)|2​η​(vmin​(q,ωn))R=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{A^{2}\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int q\,dq\sum_{n}|f(n,\mathbf{q})|^{2}\eta(v_{\rm min}(q,\omega_{n})) (81)

where

|f⁡(n,q)|2≡14​π​∫d​Ω𝐪​|f⁡(n,𝐪)|2=14​π​∫d​Ω𝐪​∑nx+ny+nz=n|⟨nx,ny,nz​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|​0⟩|2.|f(n,q)|^{2}\equiv\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d\Omega_{\mathbf{q}}\,|f(n,\mathbf{q})|^{2}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d\Omega_{\mathbf{q}}\sum_{n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z}=n}|\langle n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|0\rangle|^{2}. (82)

Here we can take the angular average over all 𝐪\mathbf{q} directions, since we are dealing with an isotropic target system. This quantity is proportional to the dynamic structure factor by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=2​πV​∑n|f⁡(n,𝐪)|2​δ​(n​ω0−ω).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{n}|f(n,\mathbf{q})|^{2}\delta(n\omega_{0}-\omega). (83)

In this case, since the spectrum of the harmonic oscillator is known exactly, we can enumerate the final states |f⟩|f\rangle in Cartesian coordinates by eigenvalues nx,ny,nzn_{x},n_{y},n_{z}, with total energy (n+12)​ω0\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\omega_{0} where n=nx+ny+nzn=n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z}. Thus vmin​(q,ωn)v_{\rm min}(q,\omega_{n}) is evaluated at ωn=n​ω0\omega_{n}=n\omega_{0}.

To compute |f⁡(n,𝐪)|2|f(n,\mathbf{q})|^{2}, consider first one Cartesian component of the matrix element, |⟨nx|ei​qx​x|0⟩|2|\langle n_{x}|e^{iq_{x}x}|0\rangle|^{2}. The perturbation operator can be written in terms of creation and annihilation operators:

exp⁡(i​qx​x)=exp⁡[i​qx2​mN​ω0​(ax+ax†)],\exp(iq_{x}x)=\exp\left[\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}\left(a_{x}+a_{x}^{\dagger}\right)\right], (84)

which has a very similar form to the exponential phonon displacement operator in Sec. III.2.2. Similar to the calculation there, we use the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, Eq. 64, with A=κ​axA=\kappa a_{x}, B=κ​ax†B=\kappa a_{x}^{\dagger}, and κ=i​qx2​mN​ω0\kappa=\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}} to obtain

exp⁡[i​qx2​mN​ω0​(ax+ax†)]=exp⁡(−qx24​mN​ω0)​exp⁡(i​qx2​mN​ω0​ax†)​exp⁡(i​qx2​mN​ω0​ax).\exp\left[\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}\left(a_{x}+a_{x}^{\dagger}\right)\right]=\exp\left(-\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{4m_{N}\omega_{0}}\right)\exp\left(\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}a_{x}^{\dagger}\right)\exp\left(\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}a_{x}\right)~. (85)

The first exponential factor is analogous to the Debye-Waller factor introduced in Sec. III.2.2. Taking the matrix element of this operator between the states ⟨nx|\langle n_{x}| and |0⟩|0\rangle, the only contribution is from the nxn_{x}th term of the middle exponential and taking the last exponential to unity. Since these operators satisfy

axn​|nx⟩=nx!​|0⟩,a^{n}_{x}|n_{x}\rangle=\sqrt{n_{x}!}|0\rangle, (86)

we obtain

⟨0​|exp⁡(−qx24​mN​ω0)​exp⁡(i​qx2​mN​ω0​ax†)​exp⁡(i​qx2​mN​ω0​ax)|​nx⟩=\displaystyle\left\langle 0\left|\exp\left(-\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{4m_{N}\omega_{0}}\right)\exp\left(\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}a_{x}^{\dagger}\right)\exp\left(\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}a_{x}\right)\right|n_{x}\right\rangle=
nx!nx!​(i​qx2​mN​ω0)nx\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{n_{x}!}}{n_{x}!}\left(\frac{iq_{x}}{\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}}\right)^{n_{x}} exp⁡(−qx24​mN​ω0).\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{4m_{N}\omega_{0}}\right)~. (87)

Taking the modulus squared of this expression gives

|⟨nx|ei​qx​x|0⟩|2=1nx!​(qx2q02)nx​exp⁡(−qx2q02),|\langle n_{x}|e^{iq_{x}x}|0\rangle|^{2}=\frac{1}{n_{x}!}\left(\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{q_{0}^{2}}\right)^{n_{x}}\exp\left(-\frac{q_{x}^{2}}{q_{0}^{2}}\right), (88)

where q0=2​mN​ω0q_{0}=\sqrt{2m_{N}\omega_{0}} is introduced for both notational convenience and physical transparency: it is the momentum spread of the ground-state wavefunction, which is given by

ϕ0(𝐩)=(πmNω0)−3/4e−p2/q02.\phi_{0}(\mathbf{p})=(\pi m_{N}\omega_{0})^{-3/4}e^{-p^{2}/q_{0}^{2}}. (89)

Eq. (88) describes a Poisson distribution in nxn_{x} with mean qx2/q02q_{x}^{2}/q_{0}^{2}. Since the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian is separable in Cartesian coordinates, we may compute the desired matrix element |⟨nx,ny,nz​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|​0⟩|2|\langle n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|0\rangle|^{2} by multiplying the three Cartesian matrix elements for nxn_{x}, nyn_{y}, and nzn_{z}. Since the sum of Poisson-distributed variables is also Poisson-distributed, the distribution of n=nx+ny+nzn=n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z} will be Poissonian, as can be verified by explicit computation:

|f(n,q)|2=1n!(q2q02)ne−q2/q02.|f(n,q)|^{2}=\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{q^{2}}{q_{0}^{2}}\right)^{n}\!\!e^{-q^{2}\!/q_{0}^{2}}. (90)

The mean occupation number for a given momentum transfer qq is

n¯q=q2q02=q22​mN​ω0=ERω0,\bar{n}_{q}=\frac{q^{2}}{q_{0}^{2}}=\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{N}\omega_{0}}=\frac{E_{R}}{\omega_{0}}, (91)

where ER=q22​mNE_{R}=\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{N}} is the recoil energy which would correspond to free-particle elastic scattering. Equivalently, the mean energy deposit n¯q​ω0\bar{n}_{q}\omega_{0} is the same as classical elastic scattering ERE_{R}, even for a bound nucleus.

In the regime where q≫q0q\gg q_{0}, the Poisson distribution becomes sharply peaked around n¯\bar{n}, approaching a delta function δ⁡(n−n¯)\delta(n-\bar{n}). This enforces the kinematic relation for elastic scattering, q=q0=2​mN​ERq=q_{0}=\sqrt{2m_{N}E_{R}} and permits the change of variables d​q=(mN/q)​d​ERdq=(m_{N}/q)dE_{R}. Taking the continuum limit with ∑n→∫dn\sum_{n}\to\int dn and n→ER/ω0n\to E_{R}/\omega_{0}, we recover precisely the spectrum for elastic nuclear scattering in Eq. (78) since

vmin=n¯q​ω0q0+q02​mχ=q02​μχ​N=mN​ER2​μχ​N2.v_{\rm min}=\frac{\bar{n}_{q}\omega_{0}}{q_{0}}+\frac{q_{0}}{2m_{\chi}}=\frac{q_{0}}{2\mu_{\chi N}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{N}E_{R}}{2\mu_{\chi N}^{2}}}. (92)

Thus, at large momentum transfer compared to the characteristic scale of the harmonic oscillator, scattering is nearly elastic and the energy deposited is given by ERE_{R}, up to small fluctuations about ERE_{R} as well as quantization of the spectrum in units of ω0\omega_{0}. There is an interesting intermediate regime as qq approaches q0q_{0} from above. Here, n¯q≳1\bar{n}_{q}\gtrsim 1 and the Poisson distribution yields order-1 fluctuations in nn and thus order-1 fluctuations in the energy deposited from DM scattering. This multi-phonon regime smoothly interpolates between large-momentum quasi-elastic scattering and small-momentum single-phonon production, and had not been considered much in the DM direct detection literature until recently [98, 99]. As a practical matter, the fact that n¯q​ω0=ER\bar{n}_{q}\omega_{0}=E_{R} means that the intuition for the kinematics of elastic scattering still hold for a bound nucleus in a harmonic potential, but the fact that the energy spectrum is quantized means that the rate for energy deposits of twice the elastic energy, 2​ω02\omega_{0}, is of the same order as the rate for ERE_{R}. This implies that for a given detector threshold, part of the multiphonon signal may be above threshold even when ERE_{R} is not. This allows for new parameter space to be probed by detectors which cannot yet achieve single-phonon sensitivity, as illustrated in Fig. 6. Another approach to the multi-phonon regime that does not use the simple harmonic oscillator model can be found in Ref. [99], which instead uses a phonon density of states, yielding similar results with the nuclear response peaked about the free recoil ERE_{R} with a width of ∼ω0​ER\sim\sqrt{\omega_{0}E_{R}}

Finally, let us consider the regime q≪q0q\ll q_{0}. Here the factor e−q2/q02≈1e^{-q^{2}/q_{0}^{2}}\approx 1, and the probability for the production of nn phonons is suppressed by (q2/q02)n(q^{2}/q_{0}^{2})^{n}. This is the same scaling as Eq. (71), following our calculation there with detailed phonon modes. However, we can see by explicit comparison with Eq. (70) that the n=1n=1 term in this simple model will not capture the target-dependent details of a solid state system. As qq drops down to keV scales and below, the particular phonon spectrum and modes of the material will play an important role in the form factors, and the assumption of a single phonon energy ω0\omega_{0} breaks down. Furthermore, the DM couplings also enter into Eq. (70). The simple q2/q02q^{2}/q_{0}^{2} scaling will not necessarily be present, depending on the DM model. We will turn to this regime next.

IV.2 Acoustic and optical phonons

For DM mass below ∼\sim 1 MeV, the maximum momentum transfer is q<1​keV<qcohq<1\ {\rm keV}<q_{\rm coh}, such that the incoherent approximation is no longer valid. Furthermore, because q≪q0q\ll q_{0}, the leading rate will generally be from single-phonon excitations, as argued above due to the (q2/q02)n(q^{2}/q_{0}^{2})^{n} scaling of nn-phonon excitations. In this section, we will give some intuition for the rate for DM to produce single phonons in solid state systems, and summarize the results of detailed numerical calculations from the literature.

First, it is worth commenting on how the kinematics of single-phonon excitations compares to elastic nuclear recoils. As discussed in Sec. III.1, there are two basic branches of phonons we could consider, acoustic and optical phonons. The comparison of DM scattering kinematics with the dispersion relations of these phonons is illustrated schematically in Fig. 4. For the acoustic phonon branch, the energy deposited must be ω∼cs​q\omega\sim c_{s}q with cs∼10−5c_{s}\sim 10^{-5}. Because the sound speed is so low compared to the DM speed, energy conservation (Eq. (9)) leads to the solution q∼2​mχ​vq\sim 2m_{\chi}v, which is the same as for sub-GeV elastic nuclear recoils. However, for acoustic phonons the energy deposited will be

ω∼2​cs​mχ​v∼2​meV×mχ100​keV.\omega\sim 2c_{s}m_{\chi}v\sim 2\,{\rm meV}\times\frac{m_{\chi}}{100\,{\rm keV}}. (93)

which is well above the elastic recoil energy for the same DM mass, ER∼10−7−10−6E_{R}\sim 10^{-7}-10^{-6} eV depending on target mass. The energy deposited into a single acoustic phonon could be made larger by using a relatively hard target material, such as SiC [103] or diamond [104] where cs≈4−5×10−5c_{s}\approx 4-5\times 10^{-5}. However, this energy deposition is still quite small: a DM particle of mass 100 keV has a typical kinetic energy of 100 meV, suggesting that acoustic phonons are not ideal in terms of matching DM kinematics.

The optical phonon branch offers a potential solution to the problem of kinematic matching. Since the dispersions are fairly flat in momentum across the BZ, Eq. (9) gives the approximate solution

q∼mχ​v±(mχ​v)2−2​mχ​ωoptical.q\sim m_{\chi}v\pm\sqrt{(m_{\chi}v)^{2}-2m_{\chi}\omega_{\rm optical}}. (94)

The typical energies are around ωoptical∼30−150\omega_{\rm optical}\sim 30-150 meV, which matches well with the total kinetic energy of DM with mass ∼10\sim 10 keV – 1 MeV. The higher energies are also favorable for experimental implementation. From this discussion, we might expect that an ideal target material would likely have a broad spectrum of optical phonon energies in the range of 1010 meV up to 150 meV, to allow kinematic matching with a broad range of DM masses. In fact, one can go further and consider systems with some amount of disorder, which further smears out the phonon spectrum and leads to broad spectrum of available modes; this idea was introduced in Ref. [105], which looked at single molecular magnet crystals as a possible direct detection target. Treating the DM coupling to specific modes is more challenging in this type of system, however. In this section, we will study only ordered crystalline lattices, where we can next specify how DM couples to individual phonon branches.

Assuming the same contact interaction as above, Eq. (75), and again applying our main rate formula Eq. 8, the rate is given by

Rχ(1−p​h)=1ρT​ρχmχ​∫d3​𝐯​fχ​(𝐯)​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​𝑑ω​π​σ¯nμχ​n2​δ​(ω+Eχ′−Eχ)​S(1−p​h)​(𝐪,ω).R_{\chi}^{(1-ph)}=\frac{1}{\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\int\,d^{3}\mathbf{v}f_{\chi}(\mathbf{v})\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,d\omega\,\frac{\pi\bar{\sigma}_{n}}{\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\delta(\omega+E^{\prime}_{\chi}-E_{\chi})\,S^{(1-ph)}(\mathbf{q},\omega). (95)

For convenience, we reproduce the single phonon dynamic structure factor:

S(1−p​h)​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle S^{(1-ph)}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =2​πΩ​∑ν|∑jfj​e−Wj​(𝐪)​i​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗2​Mj​ων,𝐪|2​δ​(ω−ων,𝐪)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\sum_{\nu}\left|\sum_{j}f_{j}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\frac{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}}{\sqrt{2M_{j}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}}}\right|^{2}\delta(\omega-\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}) (96)

with fj→Ajf_{j}\to A_{j} for equal couplings to protons and neutrons.

While the eigenmodes and dispersions of the phonon branches must be solved by DFT methods for arbitrary 𝐪\mathbf{q}, it is possible to obtain approximate results in the long-wavelength limit q≪π/aq\ll\pi/a where π/a\pi/a is the typical size of the first BZ. In this limit, we know that the acoustic phonon modes are Goldstone bosons of broken translation invariance, and that as q→0q\to 0 all the ions are displaced by the same amount for a zero-energy mode. Comparing with Eq. (49) for the displacement 𝐮{\bf u}, we see that in order for the Mj\sqrt{M_{j}} dependence to drop out, the eigenmodes for the acoustic phonons must be given by |𝐞ν,𝐪,j|=Mj/∑dMd|\mathbf{e}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}|=\sqrt{M_{j}}/\sqrt{\sum_{d}M_{d}} as q→0q\to 0; here the factor of ∑dMd\sqrt{\sum_{d}M_{d}} is just to give a normalized eigenvector, where dd sums over all ions in the unit cell. In addition, we can restrict only to the longitudinal acoustic (LA) phonon branch where 𝐞L​A,𝐪,j=𝐪^​Mj/∑dMd\mathbf{e}_{LA,\mathbf{q},j}=\hat{\mathbf{q}}\sqrt{M_{j}}/\sqrt{\sum_{d}M_{d}} because of the 𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j} dot product. This gives the LA single-phonon form factor in the long-wavelength limit:

limq→0S(1−p​h,L​A)​(𝐪,ω)≈2​πΩ​q2​|∑jAj|22​(∑dMd)​cs​q​δ​(cs​q−ω)\displaystyle\lim_{q\to 0}S^{(1-ph,LA)}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\frac{q^{2}|\sum_{j}A_{j}|^{2}}{2\,(\sum_{d}M_{d})\,c_{s}q}\delta(c_{s}q-\omega) (97)

where we have also taken e−Wj​(𝐪)≈1e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\approx 1 and an isotropic speed of sound. The form of this structure factor is similar to that computed for the harmonic oscillator model, ∝q2​A2/(2​mN​ω0)​δ​(ω−ω0)\propto q^{2}A^{2}/(2m_{N}\omega_{0})\delta(\omega-\omega_{0}) for single-phonon excitations. The difference here is that we are taking coherent sum of the couplings over the ions in the unit cell, |∑jAj|2|\sum_{j}A_{j}|^{2}, as well as dividing by unit cell mass. In addition, replacing ω0\omega_{0} with the linear dispersion of the acoustic phonons leads to a ∼q\sim q scaling for the single phonon structure factor, rather than the ∼q2\sim q^{2} scaling that was found in the toy harmonic oscillator model. Eq. (97) shows there is a coherent coupling enhancement over ions in a unit cell for acoustic phonons, and in total scales as the number of ions in the unit cell. As noted above, the kinematic matching is not ideal. If the energy threshold can be lowered to ω≥1\omega\geq 1 meV, however, there is still potentially a very strong cross section reach from single acoustic phonons, as can be seen for the ω≥1\omega\geq 1 meV line in Fig. 5.

We next turn to the optical phonon branch. For DM models where fj=Ajf_{j}=A_{j}, there is instead a destructive interference for the optical phonon coupling. To see why, let us assume Mj=Aj​mnM_{j}=A_{j}m_{n}. Then we can rewrite the structure factor as

S(1−p​h)​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle S^{(1-ph)}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =2​πΩ​∑ν|∑je−Wj​(𝐪)​i​Mj​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗2​mn2​ων,𝐪|2​δ​(ω−ων,𝐪).\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\sum_{\nu}\left|\sum_{j}e^{-W_{j}(\mathbf{q})}\frac{i\sqrt{M_{j}}\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}}{\sqrt{2m_{n}^{2}\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}}}\right|^{2}\delta(\omega-\omega_{\nu,\mathbf{q}}). (98)

In the long-wavelength limit, we can exploit the scaling of the LA phonon mode and rewrite the dot product Mj​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗\sqrt{M_{j}}\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j} as a dot product with the LA mode, 𝐞L​A,𝐪,j⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗\mathbf{e}_{LA,\mathbf{q},j}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j}. However, by definition for normal modes, the optical phonon eigenmodes are orthogonal to the acoustic phonon eigenmodes, so this dot product vanishes! Thus, the rate to produce optical phonons in this model (where the DM coupling is proportional to mass) is highly suppressed compared the acoustic phonon rate, despite the kinematic advantages. This effect was observed in the first calculations of scattering into optical modes for specific materials [106, 107], and shown to be true in general using the orthogonality argument in Ref. [108].

Since optical modes are so kinematically well-matched, it is worth obtaining the leading nonzero contribution to the rate. First, Mj=Aj​mnM_{j}=A_{j}m_{n} is not exactly true, since a nucleus is a bound state of nucleons and there is a small binding energy. Protons and neutrons also have slightly different masses. This implies a small nonzero dot product, but the effect is quite small since the deviation from Aj​mnA_{j}m_{n} is at the 10−310^{-3} level [108], and we will continue to assume Mj=Aj​mnM_{j}=A_{j}m_{n}. A larger effect results from finite qq corrections to the eigenmodes. We can see this by taking a unit cell with only two ions of mass M1,M2M_{1},M_{2}, and approximating the optical phonon eigenmode at low but finite qq:

𝐞L​O,𝐪,1≈𝐪^M2M1+M2,𝐞L​O,𝐪,2≈−𝐪^M1M1+M2e−i𝐪⋅𝐑20\mathbf{e}_{LO,\mathbf{q},1}\approx\hat{\mathbf{q}}\frac{\sqrt{M_{2}}}{\sqrt{M_{1}+M_{2}}},\quad\mathbf{e}_{LO,\mathbf{q},2}\approx-\hat{\mathbf{q}}\frac{\sqrt{M_{1}}}{\sqrt{M_{1}+M_{2}}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{2}^{0}} (99)

where we took only the longitudinal optical (LO) mode again due to the appearance of 𝐪⋅𝐞ν,𝐪,j∗\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{*}_{\nu,\mathbf{q},j} in the structure factor. As q→0q\to 0, this eigenmode is orthogonal to the LA mode, and the two ions oscillate exactly out of phase. At finite 𝐪\mathbf{q}, however, the different equilibrium positions of the ions start to be resolved compared to the wavelength of the oscillation and there is an additional relative phase factor (see also the toy model with a diatomic molecule in Ref. [108]). In this unit cell, one ion is at the origin and the other ion is located at position 𝐑20\mathbf{R}_{2}^{0}. For a cubic lattice, for instance, 𝐑20=(a/4,a/4,a/4)\mathbf{R}_{2}^{0}=(a/4,a/4,a/4) with aa the lattice constant. For q≪π/aq\ll\pi/a, we can expand the phase factor in powers of q​aqa, which gives rise to the dynamic structure factor

S(1−p​h,L​O)​(𝐪,ω)≈2​πΩ​q2​A1​A22​(M1+M2)​ωL​O​q2​a216​δ​(ω−ωL​O).S^{(1-ph,LO)}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\frac{q^{2}A_{1}A_{2}}{2(M_{1}+M_{2})\omega_{LO}}\frac{q^{2}a^{2}}{16}\delta(\omega-\omega_{LO}). (100)

where we have taken the angular average |𝐪⋅𝐑20|2≈q2​a2/16|\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{2}^{0}|^{2}\approx q^{2}a^{2}/16 and assumed a qq-independent LO phonon energy ωL​O\omega_{LO}. This has a similar form to the previous single-phonon excitation factors derived, but there is an additional (q​a)2(qa)^{2} suppression when q≪π/aq\ll\pi/a due to the destructive interference in the coupling. The structure factor thus scales as ∼q4\sim q^{4} for sub-MeV DM scattering. This behavior has been confirmed in numerical calculations [108, 107], and leads to the reduced cross-section sensitivity for producing a single optical phonon. This can be seen in Fig. 5 for mχ≲0.2m_{\chi}\lesssim 0.2 MeV and ω>20\omega>20 meV, where only scattering into a single optical phonon is possible. For masses mχ≳0.2m_{\chi}\gtrsim 0.2 MeV, larger momentum transfers are accessible and single acoustic phonon excitations also contribute to the ω>20\omega>20 meV line, leading to a similar sensitivity as the ω>1\omega>1 meV line. Given that the single-optical-phonon rate scales as q4q^{4}, it is interesting to consider whether the 2-phonon contribution to the rate is comparable, since it is expected to have the same scaling. This question was studied in Ref. [88], where it was found that the 2-phonon contribution does indeed scale as q4q^{4}, but is still smaller than the single-phonon rate, at least for sub-MeV DM.

IV.2.1 Dark photon couplings

Up to this point, we have dealt with equal proton and neutron couplings (and zero electron coupling), but it is instructive to also consider a dark photon mediator for single phonon excitations. The scaling for the acoustic and optical structure factors above is not universal and depends on the DM model couplings. The situation is quite different for dark photons, with enhanced couplings to optical phonons and a destructive interference with acoustic phonons. With this example, we will see the possibility of selecting target materials to optimize for a certain DM model.

For dark photon mediators, the DM will couple equally and oppositely to electrons and protons, similar to the ordinary photon. The electron coupling introduces some additional complication, since as the ions undergo displacements, the electrons will respond on a rapid time scale. With the same Born-Oppenheimer approximation allowing decoupling of ion and electron motion, the electron response to ion motion can be calculated with first-principles approaches, such that one can determine an effective dynamical ion charge. This leads to the definition of the Born effective charge, which is the dynamical ion charge in the long-wavelength limit. Formally, it is a charge tensor for each ion jj in the unit cell, defined as the change in polarization 𝐏\mathbf{P} resulting from a displacement to ion jj:

𝐙j∗≡Ωe​∂𝐏∂𝐮j.\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{j}\equiv\frac{\Omega}{e}\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{u}_{j}}. (101)

The Born effective charges are nonzero for polar materials, while they vanish for standard non-polar semiconductors such as Si and Ge. Let us take as a simple example of a polar material GaAs, which has a unit cell of just two ions. The Born effective charges can be approximated to be diagonal and isotropic, so that 𝐙Ga∗≈diag⁡(2.27,2.27,2.27)\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{\rm Ga}\approx{\rm diag}(2.27,2.27,2.27) and 𝐙As∗≈diag⁡(−2.27,−2.27,−2.27)\mathbf{Z}^{*}_{\rm As}\approx{\rm diag}(-2.27,-2.27,-2.27) [107], describing an effective charge sharing/splitting between the two ions. If one had modeled the Ga as donating all 3 outer shell electrons to the As, the electric charges would be +3+3 and −3-3 of the two ions, but the actual Born effective charges of +2.27+2.27 and −2.27-2.27 account for the deformation of the electron wavefunctions as the ion is displaced. Since we are dealing with a net neutral target, the sum of Born effective charge tensors for the ions must also be equal to zero. Note that aside from determining the structure factor, the polarization induced 𝐏\mathbf{P} implies that the phonon energies must be re-calculated including the electrostatic energy of this polarization. This leads to an additional contribution to the dynamical force matrix, and an increase of the LO phonon energy. For further discussion of the Born effective charges and their effect on the LO energies, see discussion in Refs. [107, 19].

Recalling the out of phase oscillations for LO modes, Eq. (99), and the fact that Ga and As have opposite Born effective charges, we see that the LO mode in a polar material can be thought of as a coherently oscillating dipole in the q→0q\to 0 limit. Thus, we can expect that the dark photon mediator primarily couples to the LO mode. To relate the dynamical ion charge to the DM couplings fjf_{j}, we must further use the fact that the ion charge will be screened in a medium, where the relevant screening factor is given by ϵ∞\epsilon_{\infty}. Here ϵ∞\epsilon_{\infty} is the long-wavelength dielectric screening at frequencies below the electron band gap but well above the optical phonon frequencies, such that ϵ∞\epsilon_{\infty} only receives contributions from valence electrons. (At frequencies below the optical phonon frequencies, the optical phonons also contribute to dielectric screening, giving rise to a low-frequency dielectric constant ϵ0\epsilon_{0}, with ϵ0>ϵ∞\epsilon_{0}>\epsilon_{\infty} in a polar material.) Then, taking fj→Zj∗/ϵ∞f_{j}\to Z^{*}_{j}/\epsilon_{\infty} and using Eq. (99), we accordingly find

S(1−p​h,L​O)​(𝐪,ω)≈2​πΩ​(Z∗)2ϵ∞2​q22​μ12​ωL​O​δ​(ω−ωL​O).S^{(1-ph,LO)}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{2\pi}{\Omega}\frac{(Z^{*})^{2}}{\epsilon_{\infty}^{2}}\frac{q^{2}}{2\mu_{12}\omega_{LO}}\delta(\omega-\omega_{LO}). (102)

where μ12\mu_{12} is the reduced mass of M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}. Because of the opposite signs of both the phonon eigenmodes and the Born effective charges, there is a coherent sum over the ions in the unit cell, in contrast to the case in Eq. (100). We find the same form and q2q^{2} scaling as the harmonic oscillator toy model, if we make the identification of the nucleus mass with μ12\mu_{12} and the replacement of the nucleus coupling with Z∗/ϵ∞Z^{*}/\epsilon_{\infty}. The structure factor in the case is also sometimes written in terms of a Fröhlich interaction which characterizes electron-phonon interactions, since the interaction of the electron is very similar to that of DM through a dark photon mediator [106, 107]. Finally, for the acoustic phonons, the opposite Born effective charges implies a destructive interference when we sum coherently over ions in the unit cell, with the structure factor going to 0 in the limit q→0q\to 0.

From these examples, we see that polar materials with large effective charges and a range of optical phonon energies are nearly-ideal target systems for DM interacting through a dark photon, since they enjoy both the kinematic matching and a coherent sum over the ions in the unit cell. For crystals with multiple optical phonon energies, it is also often the case that the highest-energy mode gives the strongest coupling [107]. This is because large effective charges also implies larger electrostatic energies associated with the phonon. For DM which couples equally to protons and neutrons, instead the rate is determined primarily through a combination of the sound speed csc_{s}, target nucleus masses, and optical phonon energies of the target system, depending on the energy threshold. Fig. 7 shows cross section sensitivities for example polar materials experiments, including GaAs and Al2O3 which are planned to be used in experimental collaborations. Studies of additional target materials can be found in Refs. [107, 74, 103, 112, 113]. Due to the resonant response, it can also be seen that single phonon excitations can give a much larger rate than DM-electron scattering (faint lines) for sub-MeV dark matter, at least in the materials studied so far; we will explore the DM-electron response more in the following section. Note that in Fig. 7, a massless dark photon mediator has been assumed where FDM​(q)=(α​me/q)2F_{\rm DM}(q)=(\alpha m_{e}/q)^{2}. For sub-MeV DM with q<q< keV, this form factor can be quite large. For massive dark photon mediators with FDM​(q)=1F_{\rm DM}(q)=1, the rate is much smaller and there is very limited sensitivity to cosmologically interesting parameter space from optical phonon excitations.

While we have mainly taken an isotropic approximation for the dynamic structure factors, another advantage of condensed matter systems is the potential directional dependence in S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega). If the DM-phonon couplings or the phonon dispersions are highly anisotropic, this will lead to a modulation of the DM scattering rate as the Earth (and thus crystal) rotates relative to the typical direction of the incoming DM. The modulation is also sensitive to the DM model details. Combined with the fact that the scattering form factor depends on the DM model, it might be possible to obtain some signal-to-background discrimination in phonon-based detection schemes, or in the case of multiple targets and a positive signal, to deduce information about the DM candidate. The directionality of single-phonon excitation rates is explored further in Refs. [107, 103, 112].

IV.3 Superfluid helium

Historically, the first efforts to exploit the particular properties of phonon modes for sub-GeV DM scattering began with an investigation of superfluid helium, a system which is different enough from solid-state lattices that it merits its own discussion. Superfluid helium-4 had been identified as an excellent candidate detector material as early as 1988 [114], just three years after the first concept for direct detection via nuclear recoil [115, 35], though the theoretical priors on WIMP DM at the time were strong enough that the prospects for sub-GeV DM were not considered. From the kinematics of nuclear scattering discussed above, it is clear that helium, as the second-lightest nucleus, is ideal for maximizing the energy transfer from GeV-mass DM [116]. To pack enough atoms into a compact volume to maximize the detection rate, one wants to use the liquid phase: 4He remains a liquid even down to absolute zero, and in fact becomes a superfluid at 2.2 K. In contrast to a solid-state system with a fixed lattice spacing aa, the disordered liquid has only an average interparticle spacing λ\lambda. For DM with mass above 5 MeV, the typical momentum transfer exceeds the inverse interparticle spacing, 1/λ≳5​keV1/\lambda\gtrsim 5\ {\rm keV}, and the scattering process can be treated as quasi-elastic, similar to the regime in Sec. IV.1. However, for lighter DM, the small momentum transfers instead imply that we are in the regime of coherent scattering. The DM will then couple to collective density oscillations in the superfluid, which are quantized into acoustic phonons. Superfluid 4He is a strongly-correlated liquid, and so the formalism in Sec. III.2.2 and Sec. IV.2 does not apply, however. We will review here the excitations in superfluid 4He  along with a few different strategies for treating this system.

The measured single-excitation spectrum ϵ⁡(𝐪)\epsilon(\mathbf{q}) of 4He (Fig. 8) contains a piece with linear dispersion at small 𝐪\mathbf{q}, ϵ⁡(𝐪)≈cs​|𝐪|\epsilon(\mathbf{q})\approx c_{s}|\mathbf{q}| where cs≈2.4×102c_{s}\approx 2.4\times 10^{2} m/s is the speed of sound, extending out to about q≃1​keVq\simeq 1\ {\rm keV}. This mode is interpreted as an acoustic phonon. DM can create a single acoustic phonon if ω=cs​|𝐪|\omega=c_{s}|\mathbf{q}|, and the kinematics is similar to that of acoustic phonons in crystals. Analogous to the discussion around Eq. 93, the typical recoil energy is

ω∼2​cs​mχ​v∼0.2​meV×mχ100​keV\omega\sim 2c_{s}m_{\chi}v\sim 0.2\,{\rm meV}\times\frac{m_{\chi}}{100\,{\rm keV}} (103)

which, unfortunately, is even more poorly kinematically matched to the DM since csc_{s} is an order of magnitude smaller for 4He than in solid-state targets. The rest of the dispersion curve contains a local maximum at q≃2​keVq\simeq 2\ {\rm keV} and ϵ⁡(𝐪)≃1.1​meV\epsilon(\mathbf{q})\simeq 1.1\ {\rm meV} (the maxon) and a local minimum at q≃4​keVq\simeq 4\ {\rm keV} (the roton), asymptoting to ϵ⁡(𝐪)≃1.5​meV\epsilon(\mathbf{q})\simeq 1.5\ {\rm meV} at large qq. We see that single-excitation production can only ever yield an energy deposit of at most ∼1\sim 1 meV, regardless of the DM mass. Eventually, at large q≫1/λq\gg 1/\lambda, the dispersion is expected to asymptote to ϵ⁡(𝐪)∼q2/(2​mHe)\epsilon(\mathbf{q})\sim q^{2}/(2m_{\rm He}), with the DM effectively scattering off single helium atoms. However, as discussed throughout this section, the dynamic structure factor also includes multi-excitation rates which grow in importance as qq grows, until they eventually converge to the quasielastic regime in Sec. IV.1. Thus, it is also possible to consider the multi-excitation rate in the regime ω>1​meV\omega>1\ {\rm meV} and q≪1​keVq\ll 1\ {\rm keV}, which is better kinematically matched to the DM and which does not require as low of a threshold as detecting single acoustic phonons. This was indeed the idea behind the recent renewal of interest in 4He as a DM detector [118, 91].

The dynamic structure factor for 4He (using conventions from [91] which differ slightly from our previous definitions) is defined as

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=1n0​∑β|⟨Ψβ|n𝐪|Ψ0⟩|2​δ​(ω−ωβ)S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{1}{n_{0}}\sum_{\beta}|\langle\Psi_{\beta}|n_{\mathbf{q}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle|^{2}\delta(\omega-\omega_{\beta}) (104)

where n0=N/Vn_{0}=N/V is the average number density, and the density operator in Fourier space is

n𝐪=1V​∑i=1Nei​𝐪⋅𝐫in_{\mathbf{q}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{i}} (105)

where 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} is the position operator for helium atom ii. As discussed in Sec. III, DM which couples to nucleons through a scalar or vector mediator will couple to the helium density operator. However, for a dark photon mediator, in the small-qq limit the DM will couple to induced dipole moments since the overall helium atom is neutral (see Eq. (33)), exactly as in the case of polar crystals. Then the correct response function will also include the polarizability of 4He, which is small. This generally results in a much less competitive reach for dark photon mediators [91].

For superfluid 4He  there are various strategies for determining the dynamic structure factor and DM scattering rate:

  1. 1.

    Directly tackle the microscopic physics to the extent possible, up to some assumptions needed to improve agreement with experimental data. There has been some recent progress in determining the dynamic structure factor including multiphonon contributions in this way, based on a many-body theory for strongly-correlated systems (e.g. [117] and references therein). This calculation roughly agrees with the measured dynamic structure factor where data is available, but extends it to the regimes needed for DM scattering. This was applied to calculate the excitation rate from DM in Ref. [91].

  2. 2.

    Use measurements of the structure factor to directly determine the rate to produce single excitations. The single-excitation rate shows up as a resonance in the experimentally measured dynamic structure factor, which can then be applied directly for the DM rate [119]. Using sum-rule arguments, it is possible to estimate the maximum size of the multi-excitation rate and obtain measurements of the multiphonon excitation in some regimes, but it is more challenging to accurately obtain the multi-excitation rate in this approach.

  3. 3.

    Write down an effective field theory (EFT) based on the spontaneous breaking of particle number symmetry, interpreting the acoustic phonon as a Goldstone mode and using measurements to fix the unknown coefficients in the effective action [120, 92, 121, 122]. This approach can be used for single and multi-excitation rates, but is limited to treating only the acoustic phonons in the excitation spectrum.

In particular, the data-driven approach of the second strategy has a close analogy in the use of the ELF to determine the response to DM-electron scattering, as we will discuss in Sec. V.3 below.

While the details of these approaches are beyond the scope of this review, we introduce some of the main ideas to illustrate the behavior of the dynamic structure factor. One perturbation theory approach starts from the original Bijl-Feyman theory for excitations in superfluid He [123, 124]. The fact that the system has a continuous translation invariance allows the possibility of a general analysis based on symmetry considerations alone, without requiring knowledge of the microscopic Hamiltonian. The Bijl-Feynman theory postulates that the approximate wavefunction for single excitations of momentum 𝐪\mathbf{q} may be constructed from the exact many-body ground state as

|𝐪⟩=1n0​S​(𝐪)​n𝐪​|Ψ0⟩.|\mathbf{q}\rangle=\frac{1}{n_{0}S(\mathbf{q})}n_{\mathbf{q}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle. (106)

One can show that |𝐪⟩|\mathbf{q}\rangle is orthogonal to the ground state, and in fact approaches an exact eigenstate of the many-body Hamiltonian as 𝐪→0\mathbf{q}\to 0, so this theory accurately describes the acoustic phonon part of the dispersion curve but begins to fail for q≳1​keVq\gtrsim 1\ {\rm keV}. The normalization of the state is enforced by the static structure factor

S⁡(𝐪)=∫d​ω​S​(𝐪,ω)=1n0​⟨Ψ0|n−𝐪​n𝐪|Ψ0⟩.S(\mathbf{q})=\int d\omega\,S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{1}{n_{0}}\langle\Psi_{0}|n_{-\mathbf{q}}n_{\mathbf{q}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle. (107)

Experimentally, S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) has been measured to be linear as q→0q\to 0, with S⁡(𝐪)=q/(2​mHe​cs)S(\mathbf{q})=q/(2m_{\rm He}c_{s}), and approaches S⁡(𝐪)→1S(\mathbf{q})\to 1 in the high qq limit. The leading order energy of the state |𝐪⟩|\mathbf{q}\rangle is given by

ϵ0​(𝐪)=⟨𝐪|δ​H|𝐪⟩=𝐪22​mHe​S​(𝐪),\epsilon_{0}(\mathbf{q})=\langle\mathbf{q}|\delta H|\mathbf{q}\rangle=\frac{\mathbf{q}^{2}}{2m_{\rm He}S(\mathbf{q})}, (108)

where δ​H=H−E0\delta H=H-E_{0} is the exact many-body Hamiltonian with the ground state energy E0E_{0} subtracted; see Ref. [91] for more details. As can be seen from Fig. 8, this Bijl-Feynman energy approaches the acoustic phonon dispersion as q→0q\to 0, while at high qq it approaches the free particle dispersion q2/(2​mHe)q^{2}/(2m_{\rm He}). However, it clearly does not reproduce the correct phonon and roton dispersion, and it is necessary to compute the full energy ϵ⁡(𝐪)\epsilon(\mathbf{q}) of the state accounting for quasiparticle interactions, such as the three-excitation vertex. These interactions also lead to multi-excitation states in the dynamic structure factor.

In general, the dynamic structure factor contains a single-quasiparticle peak and a continuum of multi-excitation states,

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=Z⁡(𝐪)​δ​(ω−ϵ⁡(𝐪))+Sm​(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=Z(\mathbf{q})\delta(\omega-\epsilon(\mathbf{q}))+S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) (109)

where Z⁡(𝐪)≈S⁡(𝐪)Z(\mathbf{q})\approx S(\mathbf{q}) in the low qq region, where Eq. (106) is a good approximation to the true single-particle eigenstates. In this region, Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) will be subdominant and the single-phonon structure factor is given by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≈q22​mHe​cs​q​δ​(ω−ϵ⁡(𝐪))≈q22​mHe​ϵ​(q)​δ​(ω−ϵ⁡(𝐪))S(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\rm He}c_{s}q}\delta(\omega-\epsilon(\mathbf{q}))\approx\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\rm He}\epsilon(q)}\delta(\omega-\epsilon(\mathbf{q})) (110)

which is precisely the same form as the single acoustic phonon structure factor computed in Eq. 97, up to the factor of 2​π/Ω2\pi/\Omega corresponding to different normalization conventions.

To obtain Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) by perturbation theory, one must next construct a set of basis states from repeated applications of the density operator, |𝐤,𝐪⟩∼n𝐤n𝐪|Ψ0⟩|\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}\rangle\sim n_{\mathbf{k}}n_{\mathbf{q}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle; the difference from the previous treatment of phonons is that the states are not automatically orthogonal, and one must orthogonalize the states by subtracting off overlaps with states of different phonon number. Unfortunately, to compute the overlap term relies on knowing the strongly correlated ground state, but a simple approach is to use the “convolution approximation” to postulate its form. With these ingredients, it is then possible to compute the three-excitation vertex ⟨𝐪−𝐤,𝐤​|δ​H|​𝐪⟩\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}|\delta H|\mathbf{q}\rangle. One can compute the renormalized energies ϵ⁡(𝐪)\epsilon(\mathbf{q}), as well as write the leading contribution to Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) in terms of two-excitation states:

Sm(2)​(𝐪,ω)=S⁡(𝐪)2​V​∫d3​𝐤(2​π)3​|⟨𝐪−𝐤,𝐤​|δ​H|​𝐪⟩|2(ϵ0​(𝐪)−ω)2​δ​(ω−ϵ0​(𝐤)−ϵ0​(𝐪−𝐤)).S^{(2)}_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{S(\mathbf{q})}{2}V\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{|\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}|\delta H|\mathbf{q}\rangle|^{2}}{(\epsilon_{0}(\mathbf{q})-\omega)^{2}}\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{0}(\mathbf{k})-\epsilon_{0}(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k})). (111)

The approach which led to Eq. (111) may be refined and improved, but even from the leading order result it is possible to reproduce the rough behavior of Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega). In the small qq limit with fixed ω\omega, Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) will be dominated by nearly back-to-back excitations with momenta 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐪−𝐤≈−𝐤\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}\approx-\mathbf{k}, with |𝐤|≫|𝐪||\mathbf{k}|\gg|\mathbf{q}| [118]. In this limit the 2-excitation structure factor scales as

Sm(2)​(𝐪,ω)∝q4S_{m}^{(2)}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\propto q^{4} (112)

at fixed ω\omega, which is physically reasonable and in agreement with the arguments of Sec. III.2.2 as well as in this section. The expected sensitivity of a 4He experiment sensitive to energy deposits ω∈[1.2,8.6]​meV\omega\in[1.2,8.6]\ {\rm meV} is shown in Fig. 5, based on theoretical calculations.

Another option to determine DM rates might be to simply use experimental data on S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) in the general rate formula Eq. (8). The dynamic structure factor may be directly measured with neutron scattering because neutrons also couple to nucleon density: by arguments very similar to the derivation of Eq. (8), the double differential neutron scattering cross section is

d2​σd​Ω​d​ω=bn2​pfpi​S​(𝐪,ω)\frac{d^{2}\sigma}{d\Omega d\omega}=b_{n}^{2}\frac{p_{f}}{p_{i}}S(\mathbf{q},\omega) (113)

where pip_{i} (pfp_{f}) is the initial (final) neutron momentum and bnb_{n} is the neutron scattering length from an individual helium nucleus. Unfortunately, experimental data on Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega), for qq below ∼\sim keV is quite limited because of the small rates, which is precisely the region needed for sub-MeV DM. The peculiar kinematics of DM make it particularly difficult to probe certain kinematic regions with standard techniques, and one must therefore use theoretical approaches validated at higher qq in these cases. Indeed, as we emphasize throughout this review, the kinematic regime relevant for sub-GeV DM has not previously been of interest to the condensed matter community, and even theoretical data may not exist at the required qq.

One can obtain qualitatively similar results for the dynamic structure factor from an EFT perspective. The presence of the acoustic phonon mode with approximately linear dispersion can be understood as a Goldstone mode for the spontaneous breaking of both particle number and time translations, via a real field ψ\psi whose vacuum expectation value (vev) represents a time-dependent chemical potential, ⟨ψ⟩=μ​t\langle\psi\rangle=\mu t, where μ\mu is the relativistic chemical potential which includes the rest mass mHem_{\rm He} in addition to the non-relativistic piece. Parameterizing the fluctuations about the expectation value in terms of a real field π\pi as

ψ⁡(𝐫,t)=μ​t+cs​μn0​π​(𝐫,t),\psi(\mathbf{r},t)=\mu t+c_{s}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{n_{0}}}\pi(\mathbf{r},t), (114)

one can write down an effective action for π\pi whose coefficients are fixed entirely in terms of the superfluid equation of state, P=P⁡(μ)P=P(\mu) or cs=cs​(P)c_{s}=c_{s}(P). This effective action has a cutoff at the momentum scale Λ≃1​keV\Lambda\simeq 1\ {\rm keV} where the dispersion ϵ⁡(𝐪)\epsilon(\mathbf{q}) deviates from linear, and thus it does not describe the maxon or roton modes, and moreover it neglects the fact that the dispersion of the phonon mode is not exactly linear but has a small positive curvature (anomalous dispersion, to be discussed further below). Since in the large-volume limit the system is translationally invariant, one can write down a relativistic EFT invariant under Poincaré transformations and the internal U(1) particle number symmetry. If we model the DM field as a complex scalar χ\chi with a dark U(1) symmetry to ensure its stability (a discrete Z2Z_{2} symmetry would also accomplish the same thing), the most general effective action which generates a spin-independent interaction between DM and 4He, at lowest order in momenta, is

Seff=∫d4​x​{P⁡(X)+Z⁡(X)​|∂μχ|2−m2​(X)​|χ|2},X=∂μψ​∂μψ.S_{\rm eff}=\int d^{4}x\,\left\{P(X)+Z(X)|\partial_{\mu}\chi|^{2}-m^{2}(X)|\chi|^{2}\right\},\qquad X=\sqrt{\partial_{\mu}\psi\partial^{\mu}\psi}. (115)

By computing the stress tensor for ψ\psi, one can verify that P⁡(X)P(X) does indeed represent the pressure of the superfluid. Expanding the Lagrangian to cubic order in π\pi, canonically normalizing π\pi and χ\chi, and taking the non-relativistic limit fixes all of the coefficients of the Lagrangian in terms of derivatives of PP, and can thus be matched to data. The result contains terms of the form π˙​(∇π)2\dot{\pi}(\nabla\pi)^{2} and π˙3\dot{\pi}^{3}, which represent 3-phonon vertices, as well as |χ|2​π˙|\chi|^{2}\dot{\pi} and |χ|2​(∂μπ)2|\chi|^{2}(\partial_{\mu}\pi)^{2} terms, which represent DM-phonon 3- and 4-point interactions, respectively. In the EFT language, the 2-phonon creation is described by two Feynman diagrams shown in Fig. 9. In the limit 𝐪→0\mathbf{q}\to 0, the intermediate phonon in the second diagram is highly off-shell, and integrating it out leads to a seemingly fine-tuned cancellation between the two amplitudes that results in the 2-phonon matrix element scaling as

|ℳ2−phonon|2∝q4ω4,|\mathcal{M}_{\rm 2-phonon}|^{2}\propto\frac{q^{4}}{\omega^{4}}, (116)

which is consistent with the result (112) from the dynamic structure factor extrapolation.1212 12 Of course, fine-tuned cancellations in low-energy Lagrangians are often manifestations of symmetries, and in this case the cancellation may be understood as a consequence of the Ward identity [125, 119]. The cancellation breaks if DM does not couple linearly to density, but the non-relativistic limit of all spin-independent scalar or vector exchange yields a coupling to density. While there may be unusual non-perturbative models for DM-SM interactions which do not couple linearly to density, all of the perturbative UV completions of spin-independent scattering yield this cancellation, which is independent of the details of the 4He EFT.
