Integrating the 2-phonon rate yields a sensitivity curve in Ref. [92] which is within a factor of 2 to the one from Ref. [91] that includes rotons and maxons, see Fig. 5.

While meV energy thresholds are already well beyond current capabilities (though they are a subject of active investigation, see Sec. VII.2), one can also explore the idea of lower energy thresholds which opens up the possibility of single-excitation production [119]. Indeed, multi-phonon production is inefficient at low qq and for sub-MeV dark matter, in the sense that it does not fully exploit the fact that the normalization of the dynamic structure factor is fixed by conservation of mass, and thus the DM scattering rate can be maximized by ensuring that the the integral in Eq. (5) contains the region where S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) has largest support.1313 13 We will see an exactly analogous situation with DM-electron scattering in semiconductors in Sec. V.3 below.. More precisely, the “ff-sum rule” is given by

∫0∞d​ω​ω​S​(𝐪,ω)=q22​mHe,\int_{0}^{\infty}\,d\omega\,\omega\,S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\rm He}}, (117)

which is valid for any momentum 𝐪\mathbf{q} and derives from the analytic properties of SS as a causal density-density correlation function. While directly measuring Sm​(𝐪,ω)S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega) at low qq is difficult with neutron probes, the single-excitation rate can be directly computed using experimentally measured quantities, with the sum rule used to constrain the remainder of the spectral weight. At low qq, the wavefunction renormalization can be expanded as

Z⁡(𝐪)=q22​mHe​ϵ​(𝐪)​(1−1.63​q2(mHe​cs)2+…),Z(\mathbf{q})=\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\rm He}\epsilon(\mathbf{q})}\left(1-1.63\frac{q^{2}}{(m_{\rm He}c_{s})^{2}}+\dots\right), (118)

where the coefficient of the q4q^{4} term is fit to neutron scattering data. The sum rule implies that

∫0∞d​ω​ω​Sm​(𝐪,ω)∫0∞d​ω​ω​S​(𝐪,ω)=1.63​q2(mHe​cs)2≃0.1​(q0.7​keV)2.\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}d\omega\,\omega\,S_{m}(\mathbf{q},\omega)}{\int_{0}^{\infty}d\omega\,\omega S(\mathbf{q},\omega)}=1.63\frac{q^{2}}{(m_{\rm He}c_{s})^{2}}\simeq 0.1\left(\frac{q}{0.7\ {\rm keV}}\right)^{2}. (119)

In other words, over 90% of the spectral weight in scattering of sub-MeV DM lies in the single-phonon part of the dynamic structure factor at q=0.7q=0.7 keV.

An interesting property of superfluid 4He is that the low-energy dispersion is not exactly linear, but is slightly convex,

ω⁡(q)≃cs​q​(1+ζA​q2+⋯)\omega(q)\simeq c_{s}q(1+\zeta_{A}q^{2}+\cdots) (120)

with ζA>0\zeta_{A}>0.1414 14 This effect may be captured in the EFT through the inclusion of higher-derivative operators. At standard volume and pressure, the dispersion curve has an inflection point at q≃0.4​keVq\simeq 0.4\ {\rm keV}, such that phonons with q<qc≃0.8​keVq<q_{c}\simeq 0.8\ {\rm keV} (ω⁡(qc)=0.68​meV\omega(q_{c})=0.68\ {\rm meV}) are unstable against decay into two lower-energy phonons. This regime is less important for the multi-excitation phonons, which have total energy well above 1 meV. For sub-meV single phonons, this will lead to a “phonon cascade” phonons reminiscent of jets or electromagnetic showers. This makes detecting individual sub-meV excitations effectively impossible, as the mean free path for splitting is on the order of cm or smaller, but if the total energy in the cascade cone could be detected, anomalous dispersion offers the intriguing possibility of localizing the event within the sample volume based on the ellipticity of the cone projected onto the surface of the detector.

V Dark Matter-Electron Scattering

The phenomenology of DM-electron scattering is dominated by the fact that electrons are bound in atomic, molecular, and solid-state systems, with wavefunctions that are very far from momentum-eigenstate plane waves. The typical length or momentum scale for electronic wavefunctions is set by the Bohr radius:

a0=1α​me=5.29×10−11​m,p0≡1a0=3.73​keV.a_{0}=\frac{1}{\alpha m_{e}}=5.29\times 10^{-11}\ {\rm m},\qquad p_{0}\equiv\frac{1}{a_{0}}=3.73\ {\rm keV}. (121)

In the ground state of the hydrogen atom, ⟨r⟩=32​a0\langle r\rangle=\frac{3}{2}a_{0}; in an larger atom, the larger value of the principal quantum number nn is partially compensated by the increased screened nuclear charge, giving a parametrically similar answer. In a molecule, the interatomic distance is set by minimizing the total energy of covalently-bonded atoms, and since the atomic wavefunctions must overlap to bond, the bond length is also of order a0a_{0}; for example, the carbon-carbon bond length in organic molecules is 0.14​nm≃2​a00.14\ {\rm nm}\simeq 2a_{0}. The same logic holds for solid-state lattices (silicon has a minimum interatomic distance of ∼4.4​a0\sim 4.4a_{0} and a lattice constant of ∼10​a0\sim 10a_{0}), and even the Fermi momentum kFk_{F} for delocalized electrons in a metal is of order p0p_{0}, since it depends on the number density of electrons and hence is set in part by the lattice spacing. The ground state position-space orbitals are localized as exp(−r/a0)\exp(-r/a_{0}), yielding momentum-space orbitals which fall off at large pp as a power law. The energies of electronic states are parametrically set by the Rydberg energy: 13.6 eV for the ionization energy of hydrogen, 𝒪⁡(10)​eV\mathcal{O}(10)\ {\rm eV} for outer-shell binding energies in noble atoms, 𝒪⁡(5)\mathcal{O}(5) eV for excitation gaps in organic molecules, and 𝒪⁡(1−5)​eV\mathcal{O}(1-5)\ {\rm eV} for semiconductor gaps. As mentioned in Sec. I, these binding energies decrease from isolated atoms to molecules to solid-state systems.

However, electron interactions can give qualitatively different behavior in specific condensed-matter systems. A key example is a superconductor, where phonons mediate a weak attractive force between electrons, binding them into Cooper pairs with a gap of 𝒪⁡(meV)\mathcal{O}({\rm meV}). There are also numerous examples of narrow-gap materials with sub-eV excitation energies: ZrTe5 (an example of a Dirac material) with a 30 meV gap, SmB6 (a Kondo insulator) with a 10 meV gap, and InSb (an otherwise ordinary semiconductor) with an accidentally small gap of 200 meV. In addition, the plasmon mode, a collective oscillation of all the valence electrons in a solid, has typical energies of 15 eV but exists solely at momenta below the scale p0p_{0}.

Comparing these scales to the typical energy and momentum scales of DM, we can refer to Fig. 1 and Eq. (9) to see that the momentum transfer required to create an excitation ω\omega must exceed

qmin=ωvmax,q_{\rm min}=\frac{\omega}{v_{\rm max}}, (122)

where vmaxv_{\rm max} is the maximum DM velocity, and we have taken the large mχm_{\chi} limit (for smaller mχm_{\chi}, qminq_{\rm min} is strictly larger). Taking vmax=v⊕+vesc≃800​km/s=2.67×10−3v_{\max}=v_{\oplus}+v_{\rm esc}\simeq 800\ {\rm km/s}=2.67\times 10^{-3}, we find

qmin≃p0​(ω10​eV)q_{\rm min}\simeq p_{0}\left(\frac{\omega}{10\ {\rm eV}}\right) (123)

while qmax=2​mχ​vmax≃p0​(mχ/0.7​MeV)q_{\rm max}=2m_{\chi}v_{\rm max}\simeq p_{0}(m_{\chi}/0.7\,{\rm MeV}). From this superficially trivial observation, we learn a number of things:

  • •

    By pure (cosmic!) coincidence, MeV–GeV DM has the correct kinematics to access the electronic response for atomic and molecular systems near where they have strong support, as shown schematically in Fig. 10. However, it can also be seen from Fig. 10 that the DM scattering kinematics is not necessarily ideally matched to the response. For example, for atomic ionization, the rate will be strongly peaked at low ionization energies, since larger ω\omega requires accessing the high-momentum tail of the electron wavefunctions which is power-law suppressed. Thus, while it is kinematically permitted for (say) 100 MeV DM to deposit all of its ∼50\sim 50 eV of kinetic energy on an atomic electron, it is extremely unlikely to do so. Similarly, this will favor scattering on the high-velocity tail of the DM velocity distribution, which implies a large increase in rate as the gap is lowered [126].

  • •

    For conventional semiconductors with 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}({\rm eV}) gaps, DM necessarily probes distance scales smaller than the lattice constant. Taking silicon as an example, with ω=1​eV\omega=1\ {\rm eV}, we find from Eq. (123) qmin≃p0/10≃(10​a0)−1q_{\rm min}\simeq p_{0}/10\simeq(10a_{0})^{-1}, which is the inverse lattice spacing. Thus, while it is true that the valence electrons are delocalized across the lattice, the particular kinematics of DM scattering weights the the quasi-localized portion of the electronic wavefunctions. Collective modes or effects are therefore less important for conventional semiconductors than for lower-gap materials.

  • •

    The peak of the plasmon mode, with q≪p0q\ll p_{0} and ω≃15​eV\omega\simeq 15\ {\rm eV}, is kinematically inaccessible to halo DM. As we will see in Sec. V.3 below, the plasmon is responsible for the bulk of the support of the loss function at low momentum, while the loss function at high momentum is spread out over a larger ω\omega range. In this sense, conventional materials are “inefficient” with respect to DM scattering. This is analogous to the case of multi-phonon excitations in superfluid helium discussed in Sec. IV.3 above, rather than the resonant single-phonon excitations discussed in Sec. IV.2.

  • •

    Accessing the true long-range behavior of delocalized electrons requires a narrow-gap material, most of which have rather exotic electronic properties. Since these narrow gaps are mandatory to probe sub-MeV DM which carries sub-eV kinetic energies, the search for novel materials with the required electronic properties, involving close collaboration with condensed matter physicists, is a key component of the active research in light DM detection.

The peculiar kinematics of DM also mean that the regime of the electronic response function accessible to DM is quite under-explored experimentally. For example, the plasmon has been extremely well-studied at energies near the peak, but much less attention has been given to the low-energy tail which is the only part accessible to DM in conventional materials. For heavier DM, the high momentum regime dominates, for which there is limited experimental data. Similarly, atomic wavefunctions are often studied using photoabsorption, where ω=q\omega=q, but DM probes the kinematically-distinct regime ω≃10−3​q\omega\simeq 10^{-3}q. At present, almost all of the predictions for DM-electron scattering rates rely on primarily theoretical determinations of the response, using the tools described in Sec. III.1, with limited direct experimental input for calibration. That said, the arguments of Sec. III.2 show that, at least for the dark photon model, the relevant dynamic structure factor (namely, the ELF) may be directly measured with electromagnetic probes such as electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) or X-ray scattering, which can be configured to access the correct kinematic regime. Dedicated measurements in the coming years, on novel and conventional materials alike, will greatly reduce the systematic uncertainty associated with DM-electron scattering.

To give a sense of the available parameter space for DM-electron scattering, Fig. 11 shows the current leading limits from several experiments, each of which will be discussed more below and in Sec. VII.1515 15 These limits are derived from published results, but many of them are based on theoretical rate predictions which neglect important many-body effects, as pointed out in [132, 131, 128, 113] and to be discussed further below. The two models correspond to spin-independent scattering through a heavy mediator (left panel) or light mediator (right panel). Constraints are shown alongside the relic density targets from the freeze-out and freeze-in mechanisms and the “neutrino floor” (see Sec. VII.5) for a silicon target with a 100 kg-yr exposure and a 1-electron threshold. Fig. 12 shows the background-free projected limits from a number of theory proposals, many of which would allow access to the remaining cosmologically-allowed sub-GeV parameter space.

V.1 Atomic ionization

V.1.1 Hydrogen toy model

The first application of dark matter-electron scattering involved electron ionization in liquid xenon [18, 133], but to illustrate the essential features we will start first with a simpler toy example, dark matter scattering off a single hydrogen atom [134, 135]. Throughout this section, we will take the benchmark dark photon model, where DM couples to both protons and electrons with a spin-independent potential. Summing over all target atoms (or nuclei), the dynamic structure factor is

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=2​π​NnucV​∑f|⟨f|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫N−ei​𝐪⋅𝐫e|0⟩|2​δ​(Ef−E0−ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi N_{\rm nuc}}{V}\sum_{f}|\langle f|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{N}}-e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{e}}|0\rangle|^{2}\delta(E_{f}-E_{0}-\omega) (124)

where 𝐫N\mathbf{r}_{N} and 𝐫e\mathbf{r}_{e} are the nuclear and electronic coordinates, respectively, and |f⟩|f\rangle represents an excited electronic state of the atom. In the approximation where the nucleus is infinitely heavy and thus stationary, we may set 𝐫N=0\mathbf{r}_{N}=0. In that limit, nuclear scattering does not contribute to electronic excitation when |f⟩≠|0⟩|f\rangle\neq|0\rangle; we will see in Sec. VI below how this picture is modified when the finite mass of the nucleus is taken into account.

The excited electron state |f⟩|f\rangle may be either a bound state or a continuum state, the latter of which corresponds to an ionized electron. Since the formalism of atomic electron scattering is typically applied to liquid noble element detectors which are sensitive to ionized electrons, we will focus on the continuum states and return to the discrete spectrum of bound states in Sec. V.2 below. The initial state is simply the ground state of the hydrogen atom, ψ100(𝐫)=2a0−3/2e−r/a0\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r})=2a_{0}^{-3/2}e^{-r/a_{0}}. Excited states are labeled by a wavevector 𝐤\mathbf{k}, so the sum over |f⟩|f\rangle turns into an integral, and the structure factor becomes

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=2​π​NnucV​∫d3​𝐤(2​π)3​δ​(E𝐤−E0−ω)​|f0→𝐤​(𝐪)|2S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{2\pi N_{\rm nuc}}{V}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\delta(E_{\mathbf{k}}-E_{0}-\omega)|f_{0\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2} (125)

where

f0→𝐤​(𝐪)=∫d3​𝐫​ψ𝐤∗​(𝐫)​ψ100​(𝐫)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫f_{0\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})=\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}\ \psi^{*}_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\psi_{100}(\mathbf{r})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}} (126)

is the atomic form factor for transitions between the ground state and the continuum state 𝐤\mathbf{k}. Asymptotically far away from the nucleus, the final-state electron behaves as a free particle, so we have absorbed an extra factor of V\sqrt{V} inside ψ𝐤∗​(𝐫)\psi^{*}_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}), such that it behaves as ψ𝐤∗​(𝐫)∝ei​𝐤⋅𝐫\psi^{*}_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\propto e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} as r→∞r\to\infty. Similarly, we may define 𝐤\mathbf{k} through the energy of the continuum state as E𝐤=k22​meE_{\mathbf{k}}=\frac{k^{2}}{2m_{e}}. Typically we are interested in the energy spectrum of ionized electrons d​R/d​EerdR/dE_{\rm er}, so using d​Eer=d​E𝐤=k​d​k/medE_{\rm er}=dE_{\mathbf{k}}=kdk/m_{e}, we may trade the integral over kk for an integral over EerE_{\rm er}. Collecting the various normalization factors, and decomposing the outgoing wavefunction into spherical waves with angular quantum numbers l′l^{\prime} and m′m^{\prime}, it is convenient to define an ionization form factor,

|fion​(k,q)|2=∑l′,m′2​k3(2​π)3​|f0→k,l′,m′​(𝐪)|2|f_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2}=\sum_{l^{\prime},m^{\prime}}\frac{2k^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}|f_{0\to k,l^{\prime},m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2} (127)

where the factor of 2 accounts for spin degeneracy. The radial part R~k​l\widetilde{R}_{kl} of the ionized wavefunctions is normalized as

∫d​r​r2​R~k​l∗​(r)​R~k′​l′​(r)=(2​π)3​1k2​δl​l′​δ​(k−k′),\int dr\,r^{2}\,\widetilde{R}^{*}_{kl}(r)\,\widetilde{R}_{k^{\prime}l^{\prime}}(r)=(2\pi)^{3}\frac{1}{k^{2}}\delta_{ll^{\prime}}\delta(k-k^{\prime})\,, (128)

so that R~k​l​(r)\widetilde{R}_{kl}(r) itself is dimensionless, and therefore so is fionf_{\rm ion}. Using Eq. 11 since the target system is spherically symmetric, we obtain the experimental quantity of interest, the total differential rate per unit detector mass,

d​Rd​ln⁡Eer=NT​ρχmχ​σ¯e8​μχ​e2​∫d​q​q​|FDM​(q)|2​|fion​(k,q)|2​η​(vmin),\frac{dR}{d\ln E_{\rm er}}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{8\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int dq\,q\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2}\eta(v_{\rm min}), (129)

where for electron scattering

vmin=Eer+|E0|q+q2​mχv_{\rm min}=\frac{E_{\rm er}+|E_{0}|}{q}+\frac{q}{2m_{\chi}} (130)

and the form factor for a dark photon mediator FDM​(q)F_{\rm DM}(q) was defined in Eq. (25). NTN_{T} is again the number of target nuclei per unit detector mass, and E0=−13.6​eVE_{0}=-13.6\ {\rm eV} is the binding energy of hydrogen.

If we approximate the outgoing state ψ𝐤\psi_{\mathbf{k}} as a pure plane wave e−i𝐤⋅𝐫e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}, we may use the decomposition of plane waves into spherical wavefunctions to compute the form factor analytically for l′=m′=0l^{\prime}=m^{\prime}=0 [135]:

2​k3(2​π)3​|f0→k,0,0​(𝐪)|2=64​(k​a0)3π​[a04​(k2−q2)2+2​a02​(k2+q2)+1]2(hydrogen,plane−wave​final​state)\frac{2k^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}|f_{0\to k,0,0}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}=\frac{64(ka_{0})^{3}}{\pi[a_{0}^{4}(k^{2}-q^{2})^{2}+2a_{0}^{2}(k^{2}+q^{2})+1]^{2}}\quad{\rm(hydrogen,\ plane-wave\ final\ state)} (131)

This function has the most support at k≃q≃1/a0k\simeq q\simeq 1/a_{0}, reflecting the fact that the characteristic momentum scale for electrons in the hydrogen atom is 1/a01/a_{0}. Of course, since DM must have at least |E0||E_{0}| of kinetic energy to ionize hydrogen, ionization is only kinematically allowed for mχ≳10​MeVm_{\chi}\gtrsim 10\ {\rm MeV}, for which q=1/a0q=1/a_{0} is kinematically allowed as well. This intuition typically holds for more complicated atoms – the peak of the structure factor is kinematically accessible – but not necessarily for molecular or solid-state excitation, as we will see below.

Note also that fion​(k,q)f_{\rm ion}(k,q) in (131) does not vanish as q→0q\to 0, as required by orthogonality of initial and final states. This unphysical behavior is simply because the plane-wave approximation is sufficient far from the origin, but due to the localization of the initial state, the integrand of the transition form factor (126) is dominated by the region close to the origin. Indeed, the Coulomb potential of the nucleus distorts the continuum wavefunction, which we can account for by choosing the final-state wavefunction to be the exact positive-energy solution of the Coulomb potential. Writing ψ𝐤​(𝐫)\psi_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) in spherical coordinates as Ylm​(θ,ϕ)​R~k​l​(r)Y^{m}_{l}(\theta,\phi)\widetilde{R}_{kl}(r), the radial function is [136]

R~k​l​(r)=(2​π)3/2​2π​|Γ⁡(l+1+i​Zk​a0)|​eπ​Z2​k​a0(2​l+1)!​ei​k​r​F11​(l+1+i​Zk​a0,2​l+2,2​i​k​r),\widetilde{R}_{kl}(r)=(2\pi)^{3/2}\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left|\Gamma\left(l+1+\frac{iZ}{ka_{0}}\right)\right|e^{\frac{\pi Z}{2ka_{0}}}}{(2l+1)!}e^{ikr}\,{}_{1}F_{1}\left(l+1+\frac{iZ}{ka_{0}},2l+2,2ikr\right), (132)

where Γ\Gamma is the gamma function, F11{}_{1}F_{1} is the confluent hypergeometric function, and we leave the nuclear charge ZZ arbitrary to facilitate later comparison with larger hydrogenic atoms. Since this is an eigenstate of the same potential which determines the ground state, it is automatically orthogonal to ψ100\psi_{100} when Z=1Z=1. The ratio of the wavefunction at the origin to the wavefunction at infinity is

|R~k​l​(r=0)R~k​l​(r=∞)|2=2​π​Zk​a0​11−e−2πZ/(ka0),\left|\frac{\widetilde{R}_{kl}(r=0)}{\widetilde{R}_{kl}(r=\infty)}\right|^{2}=\frac{2\pi Z}{ka_{0}}\frac{1}{1-e^{-2\pi Z/(ka_{0})}}, (133)

where the right-hand side is also known as the Fermi factor. It diverges as k→0k\to 0, reflecting the infinite range of the pure Coulomb potential. This increases the form factor at small kk compared to the plane-wave approximation [18, 137], an effect known as Sommerfeld enhancement in the context of beta decay.

However, using the exact radial wavefunction in Eq. (132), the ionization form factor can be obtained as [134]

|fion​(k,q)|2=512​Z6​k2​q2​a04​((3​q2+k2)​a02+Z2)​exp⁡[−2​Zk​a0​tan−1⁡(2​Z​k​a0(q2−k2)​a02+Z2)]OPEN3​((q+k)2​a02+Z2))3​((q−k)2​a02+Z2)3​(1−e−2​π​Zk​a0)(hydrogen,exact)|f_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2}=\frac{512Z^{6}k^{2}q^{2}a_{0}^{4}((3q^{2}+k^{2})a_{0}^{2}+Z^{2})\exp\left[-\frac{2Z}{ka_{0}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2Zka_{0}}{(q^{2}-k^{2})a_{0}^{2}+Z^{2}}\right)\right]}{3((q+k)^{2}a_{0}^{2}+Z^{2}))^{3}((q-k)^{2}a_{0}^{2}+Z^{2})^{3}(1-e^{-\frac{2\pi Z}{ka_{0}}})}\quad{\rm(hydrogen,\ exact)} (134)

which vanishes as q→0q\to 0 as expected. The dynamic structure factor for ionization of atomic hydrogen is then given by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=π​natom​mek2×|fion​(k,q)|2,k=2​me​(ω−|E0|).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\pi n_{\rm atom}\frac{m_{e}}{k^{2}}\times|f_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2},\quad k=\sqrt{2m_{e}(\omega-|E_{0}|)}. (135)

We plot this in Fig. 13, as compared with the kinematic restriction for DM scattering, which requires us to be to the right of the dashed line. As discussed in the introduction to this section, this implies that we obtain the largest rates for DM on the tail of the velocity distribution and favoring low ω\omega. Furthermore, it is clear that atomic hydrogen is not an ideal direct detection target given that the region where the dynamic structure factor is largest is not entirely accessible to DM.

V.1.2 Noble atoms

For DM scattering in many-electron atoms, we must contend with the fact that there are no longer exact solutions for the wavefunctions, and electron interaction and exchange effects can generically no longer be ignored. One approach is to use the Hartree-Fock approximation to construct the approximate many-electron bound-state wavefunctions as a Slater determinant of single-particle orbitals ψi\psi_{i}, i=1,…,Nei=1,\dots,N_{e}:

Ψ(𝐫1,𝐫2,…,𝐫Ne)=|ψ1⋯ψNe|≡1Ne!∑σ∈SNe(−1)σψσ⁡(1)(𝐫1)⋯ψσ⁡(Ne)(𝐫Ne)\Psi(\mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{r}_{N_{e}})=|\psi_{1}\cdots\psi_{N_{e}}|\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{e}!}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{N_{e}}}(-1)^{\sigma}\psi_{\sigma(1)}(\mathbf{r}_{1})\cdots\psi_{\sigma(N_{e})}(\mathbf{r}_{N_{e}}) (136)

where SNeS_{N_{e}} is the permutation group on NeN_{e} elements and σ\sigma is a permutation with sign (−1)σ(-1)^{\sigma}. The matrix element for a single ionized electron will involve a new Slater determinant state Ψ′=|ψ1​…​ψi−1​ψ′​ψi+1​…​ψNe|\Psi^{\prime}=|\psi_{1}\dots\psi_{i-1}\psi^{\prime}\psi_{i+1}\dots\psi_{N_{e}}| with one of the ψi\psi_{i} replaced by some continuum wavefunction ψ′\psi^{\prime}. As long as all of the single-particle orbitals are orthonormal, the only nonvanishing terms will contain transitions between ψi\psi_{i} and ψ′\psi^{\prime}:

⟨Ψ′|∑i=1Neei​𝐪⋅𝐫i|Ψ⟩=⟨ψ′|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|ψ⟩.\langle\Psi^{\prime}|\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{i}}|\Psi\rangle=\langle\psi^{\prime}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|\psi\rangle. (137)

Thus, in the Hartree-Fock approximation one can compute the scattering rate using single-particle orbitals, with many-body effects included in the chosen form of the orbitals.

To generalize the formalism for hydrogen to noble atoms with filled shells (the case most relevant for experiments probing atomic electron scattering, all of which are currently using noble liquid targets), we may define the atomic form factor for the (n,l)(n,l) orbital as

fn​l→𝐤​(𝐪)=∑m|∫d3​𝐫​ψ𝐤∗​(𝐫)​ψn​l​m​(𝐫)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|2,f_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})=\sum_{m}\left|\int d^{3}\mathbf{r}\,\psi^{*}_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\,\psi_{nlm}(\mathbf{r})\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\right|^{2}, (138)

where we have assumed approximate degeneracy in mm and summed incoherently over transitions of individual orbitals. Using spherical symmetry and decomposing the outgoing wavefunction into spherical waves, we can then perform the sum over mm and write the ionization form factor as an integral over the radial functions,

|fionn​l​(k,q)|2=4​k3(2​π)3​∑l′=0∞∑L=|l′−l|l′+l(2​l+1)​(2​l′+1)​(2​L+1)​[ll′L000]2​|∫d​r​r2​R~k​l′​(r)​Rn​l​(r)​jL​(q​r)|2,|f^{nl}_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2}=\frac{4k^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{l^{\prime}=0}^{\infty}\sum_{L=|l^{\prime}-l|}^{l^{\prime}+l}(2l+1)(2l^{\prime}+1)(2L+1)\left[\begin{matrix}l&l^{\prime}&L\\ 0&0&0\\ \end{matrix}\right]^{2}\left|\int dr\,r^{2}\widetilde{R}_{kl^{\prime}}(r)R_{nl}(r)j_{L}(qr)\right|^{2}\,, (139)

where R~k​l′​(r)\widetilde{R}_{kl^{\prime}}(r) and Rn​lR_{nl} are the final-state and initial-state radial wavefunctions, respectively, jLj_{L} is the spherical Bessel function of order LL, and the term in brackets is the Wigner-3​j3j symbol evaluated at m1=m2=m3=0m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}=0.1616 16 Here we have included the factor of 2 for spin degeneracy in Eq. (139) rather than Eq. (138), but this is simply a matter of convention. In practice, the sum over l′l^{\prime} may be cut off at some moderate value l′≃10l^{\prime}\simeq 10 once the sum converges to the desired accuracy. The total scattering rate is an incoherent sum over all |fionn​l​(k,q)|2|f^{nl}_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2} for different (n,l)(n,l),

d​Rd​ln⁡Eer=NT​ρχmχ​σ¯e8​μχ​e2​∑n,l∫d​q​q​|FDM​(q)|2​|fionn​l​(k,q)|2​η​(vmin),\frac{dR}{d\ln E_{\rm er}}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{8\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\sum_{n,l}\int dq\,q\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f^{nl}_{\rm ion}(k,q)|^{2}\eta(v_{\rm min}), (140)

with

vmin=Eer+|En​l|q+q2​mχv_{\rm min}=\frac{E_{\rm er}+|E_{nl}|}{q}+\frac{q}{2m_{\chi}} (141)

where En​lE_{nl} is the binding energy of the (n,l)(n,l) shell.

In the Hartree-Fock approximation, the radial wavefunctions for each orbital can be expressed in a basis of Slater-type orbitals with effective charges Zj​lZ_{jl} and coefficients Cj​l​nC_{jln} as [138]

Rn​l(r)=a0−3/2∑jCj​l​n(2​Zj​l)nj​l′+1/2(2​nj​l′)!(ra0)nj​l′−1e−Zj​lr/a0.R_{nl}(r)=a_{0}^{-3/2}\sum_{j}C_{jln}\frac{(2Z_{jl})^{n^{\prime}_{jl}+1/2}}{\sqrt{(2n^{\prime}_{jl})!}}\left(\frac{r}{a_{0}}\right)^{n^{\prime}_{jl}-1}e^{-Z_{jl}r/a_{0}}\,. (142)

These wavefunctions are known as Roothaan-Hartree-Fock (RHF) wavefunctions after a standard technique in quantum chemistry for solving the Hartree-Fock equations. Since Ref. [138] does not provide parameterizations of the continuum wavefunctions, the earlier applications of this formalism [133, 139] had to supply the final-state wavefunctions externally, which were not guaranteed to be orthogonal to the bound states and thus neglect many-body effects in a possibly important way.1717 17 In the earliest literature [18], a plane-wave approximation was used for computational simplicity, along with choosing a rather ad-hoc ZeffZ_{\rm eff} and adding in a Fermi factor by hand. In the most recent analyses used by the XENON [100] and Panda-X [140] (liquid Xe), and DarkSide [141] (liquid Ar) collaborations, the following prescription for the outgoing wavefunctions was used: pretend the bound-state orbital Rn​lR_{nl} is a bound state of a pure Coulomb potential −Zeffn​l/r-Z_{\rm eff}^{nl}/r (rather than the self-consistent potential giving rise to the RHF wavefunctions), and determine Zeffn​lZ_{\rm eff}^{nl} by matching the Coulomb energy eigenvalue to the RHF eigenvalue. For all transitions from the n​lnl state, one then uses this Zeffn​lZ_{\rm eff}^{nl} to construct the outgoing radial functions R~k′​l′​(r)\widetilde{R}_{k^{\prime}l^{\prime}}(r); note this does imply different outgoing radial functions used for different transitions. Fig. 14 shows the ionization form factors (139) and ionization spectrum (140) for the outermost shell in argon, for different choices of the outgoing wavefunctions and/or Fermi factors. The rate peaks at Eer≃p02/(2​me)=9​eVE_{\rm er}\simeq p_{0}^{2}/(2m_{e})=9\ {\rm eV}, largely independent of the DM mass, as anticipated from the arguments at the beginning of this section.

As the atomic number of an atom increases, relativistic effects become more important. These can be incorporated [142, 132] with the Dirac-Hartree-Fock approximation, for which a public code, FAC, exists to calculate both the bound and continuum wavefunctions from a self-consistent potential [143], ensuring orthogonality.1818 18 That said, FAC is unable to reproduce measured binding energies of outer-shell electrons in xenon at the 20% level, which strongly affects the sensitivity near threshold; the private code of Ref. [132] utilized the relativistic random-phase approximation and benchmarked the wavefunctions by matching the measured ionization energies of each shell. The combination of relativistic and many-body effects (which are expected to be important for excited states) in xenon produces a spectrum which differs by almost an order of magnitude at both small and large ionization energies, suppressing the rate at small energies but drastically increasing the tail at large energies, which can potentially have a large impact on experimental searches [132]. As of yet there is no direct measurement of the ionization form factors of xenon and argon in the relevant kinematic regime for sub-GeV DM-electron scattering, and thus each of the above approximations for the wavefunctions must be considered to carry some unquantified systematic uncertainty.

V.1.3 General atomic response

All of the above discussion has assumed that the DM-electron interaction Hamiltonian Δ​Hχ​e\Delta H_{\chi e} is independent of both the DM and electron spins. As shown in Eq. (20), this is true in the 𝐯→0\mathbf{v}\to 0 limit for the dark photon model, but in a bottom-up approach there are 14 non-relativistic operators at linear order in 𝐯\mathbf{v} and quadratic order in 𝐪\mathbf{q} consistent with Galilean invariance and momentum conservation which can depend on various products of momentum and spin, as shown schematically in Eq. (30). Among the incoming and outgoing DM and electron states, there are two independent momenta, which can be taken to be 𝐪\mathbf{q} and

𝐯el⟂=𝐯−𝐪2​μχ​e−𝐤me,\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}=\mathbf{v}-\frac{\mathbf{q}}{2\mu_{\chi e}}-\frac{\mathbf{k}}{m_{e}}, (143)

where 𝐤\mathbf{k} is the initial-state electron momentum (or the relevant Fourier component of the wavefunction, if the initial state is not a momentum eigenstate). The notation and definition are inherited from the case of elastic nuclear scattering, where 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0 for a nucleus at rest, and 𝐯el⟂⋅𝐪=0\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp}\cdot\mathbf{q}=0 for elastic scattering.

Specializing to the case of DM-electron scattering in atoms [71], the possible dependence of Δ​Hχ​e\Delta H_{\chi e} on 𝐯el⟂\mathbf{v}_{\rm el}^{\perp} leads to a second vectorial atomic form factor

𝐟1→2​(𝐪)=∫d3​k(2​π)3​ψ2∗​(𝐤+𝐪)​(𝐤me)​ψi​(𝐤)\mathbf{f}_{1\to 2}(\mathbf{q})=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\psi_{2}^{*}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})\left(\frac{\mathbf{k}}{m_{e}}\right)\psi_{i}(\mathbf{k}) (144)

which appears in the total scattering rate through three additional atomic response functions. Schematically, these are

W2∼𝐪me​fn​l→𝐤​(𝐪)​𝐟n​l→𝐤​(𝐪),W3∼|𝐟n​l→𝐤​(𝐪)|2,W4∼|𝐪me⋅𝐟n​l→𝐤​(𝐪)|2,W_{2}\sim\frac{\mathbf{q}}{m_{e}}f_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{f}_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q}),\ \ W_{3}\sim|\mathbf{f}_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2},\ \ W_{4}\sim\left|\frac{\mathbf{q}}{m_{e}}\cdot\mathbf{f}_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}, (145)

where W1W_{1} is proportional to the ionization form factor |fn​l→𝐤​(𝐪)|2|f_{nl\to\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{q})|^{2} and is the sole response function which governs spin-independent scattering. Since |𝐪|≲me|\mathbf{q}|\lesssim m_{e} for sub-GeV DM, and atomic wavefunctions have support peaked at |𝐤|≃1/a0=α​me≪me|\mathbf{k}|\simeq 1/a_{0}=\alpha m_{e}\ll m_{e}, these additional form factors are typically strongly suppressed compared to the standard atomic form factor. In addition, these response functions are multiplied in the rate by additional powers of 𝐯\mathbf{v}, further suppressing the rate. The only exception is the standard “spin-dependent” operator 𝐒e⋅𝐒χ\mathbf{S}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{\chi}, which does not depend on any powers of momentum and hence scales parametrically like spin-independent scattering. Recently, Ref. [144] provided a many-body treatment of these spin-dependent operators.

Depending on the particle nature of the DM, spin-independent scattering may not be the leading contribution to DM-electron interactions, and thus these general atomic responses may offer the possibility of distinguishing between DM models (though at the cost of a suppressed rate compared to the spin-independent expectation) [145]. One example is if DM couples to electromagnetism through electric dipole, magnetic dipole, or “anapole” moments; if DM is a Majorana fermion, a spin-1/2 particle that is its own antiparticle, the anapole moment is the only nonzero coupling because the electric and magnetic dipoles vanish identically. In this scenario, the mediator between DM and electrons is just the photon itself, but DM couples directly to the Maxwell field strength tensor Fμ​νF_{\mu\nu}, giving additional spin and velocity dependence to Δ​Hχ​e\Delta H_{\chi e}. By exploiting the differences in the ionization spectra in xenon inherited from the various spin-dependent atomic response functions, Ref. [145] showed that observation of 𝒪⁡(100−1000)\mathcal{O}(100-1000) events can reject the Majorana DM hypothesis.

V.2 Molecular excitation and scintillation

Molecular systems offer several unique advantages for DM-electron scattering. First, consistent with the general principle that closer interatomic spacing leads to smaller binding energies, molecules can have electronic states with smaller separation than the ionization energies of the isolated outer-shell atomic electrons. Second, unlike noble atoms, molecules are naturally anisotropic, and the breaking of spherical symmetry can lead to pronounced daily modulation of the event rate which is a smoking-gun signal of DM.1919 19 Similar effects are present when electrons are ionized from two-dimensional materials like graphene [146] or carbon nanotubes [147]. Third, organic compounds in particular have a long history of use as scintillation detectors for high-energy particles [148]: when a molecule de-excites from an excited electronic state, it emits a photon, which is wavelength-shifted with respect to the excitation energy through internal relaxation (for example, via vibrational levels) such that the probability of the photon exiting the sample (rather than being reabsorbed) is large. This property has previously been proposed to detect nuclear scattering events [149, 93], where the electronic excitation occurs due to collisions between molecules, but it was pointed out in [150, 127] that the same scintillation effect may be used to search for direct electron scattering.

The key property which differentiates a condensed-matter molecular system (either a liquid, or a molecular crystal with very weak intermolecular correlations) from a generic semiconductor or insulator is that the electrons are not delocalized across the entire sample but are confined to individual molecules. Focusing on organic aromatic compounds in particular, the general structure for molecules with delocalized electron systems is a planar network of carbon-carbon double and single bonds in which hexagonal rings are present. Fig. 15 shows as an example the structure of trans-stilbene (t-stilbene). The partially-filled 2p shell in carbon can accommodate a handful of arrangements of 4 bonds and, in particular, the sp2 hybridized configuration (formed from linear combinations of 2s and 2p orbitals) allows for two single bonds and one double bond. The three sp2 hybrid orbitals responsible for the so-called σ\sigma-bonding, which runs along the interatomic axis, gives these molecules their planar nature. By contrast, the unhybridized 2pz orbitals extend out of the plane and form π\pi-bonds through lateral overlap. The alternating π\pi-bonds form a delocalized electronic system whose dynamics can be considered independently from the tightly bound σ\sigma-bonds that make up the rigid skeleton of the molecule; the electrons in the π\pi system are the analog of the valence electrons in a solid-state system.

Ignoring electron correlation and repulsion effects for the moment, and considering only nearest-neighbor bonding interactions, the ground state and lowest-lying electronic states of the many-body system are well-described by linear combinations of 2pz orbitals, which represent π\pi electrons delocalized across the molecule:

Ψi=∑jcij​ϕ2​pz​(𝐫−𝐑j),ϕ2​pz​(𝐫)=Zeff525​π​a03​r​cos⁡θa0​exp⁡(−Zeff​r2​a0),\Psi_{i}=\sum_{j}c_{i}^{j}\phi_{2p_{z}}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{j}),\qquad\phi_{2p_{z}}(\mathbf{r})=\sqrt{\frac{Z_{\rm eff}^{5}}{2^{5}\pi a_{0}^{3}}}\frac{r\cos\theta}{a_{0}}\exp\left(\frac{-Z_{\rm eff}r}{2a_{0}}\right), (146)

where jj runs over all the carbon atoms in the molecule with positions 𝐑j\mathbf{R}_{j} and Zeff≈3.15Z_{\rm eff}\approx 3.15 is the effective nuclear charge of carbon seen by the 2pz orbital. These states are known as Hückel molecular orbitals (HMOs). Typical excitation energies from the ground state to the lowest excited state are Δ​E≃4.5​eV\Delta E\simeq 4.5\ {\rm eV} in benzene (6 carbon atoms) and Δ​E≃4.2​eV\Delta E\simeq 4.2\ {\rm eV} in t-stilbene (14 carbon atoms), about a factor of 2 lower than the outer-shell ionization energy in xenon, which allows organic scintillators to probe lower-mass DM compared to noble liquids.

Due to the relatively small number of electrons involved in the low-lying states (one per carbon atom), a fairly complete treatment of the correlation and repulsion effects is feasible for molecules with 𝒪⁡(10)\mathcal{O}(10) carbon atoms, using the Hartree-Fock approximation in the HMO basis. Indeed much of the work in understanding organic compounds was done in the quantum chemistry literature in the 1960’s with results that can be borrowed almost verbatim, as detailed in [150, 127]. Another useful result from this literature is a semi-empirical method which may be used to avoid the computational complexity of Hartree-Fock for larger molecules [151, 152, 153, 154]. First, the coefficients cjic_{j}^{i} of the HMOs are fixed by assuming that nearest-neighbor interactions dominate and empirically fitting the coefficients such that the eigenspectrum matches the observed spectrum of the desired molecule; off-diagonal elements are related to bond lengths and diagonal elements can be interpreted as an effective nuclear charge. Degeneracies are resolved by requiring each HMO to transform in an irreducible representation of the symmetry group of the molecule in question, known as the point group which keeps the origin fixed. To obtain the many-body wavefunction, antisymmetry is enforced with a variant of the Hartree-Fock approximation, where the ground state is constructed as a Slater determinant of the lowest-energy HMOs in a spin-singlet configuration, and the excited states are constructed by replacing one of the HMOs with a higher-energy orbital in the antisymmetrized wavefunction. Finally, electron-electron interactions are treated as perturbations which mix states with the same symmetries under the point group. This procedure, which focuses on just the bound-electron spin singlet configurations, suffices for practical applications because the singlet states are overwhelmingly responsible for the experimentally-observable scintillation transitions.

As with the case of atomic scattering, the transition form factor can be reduced to calculating matrix elements with single-particle orbitals at different sites, because each excited electron state can be written as linear combinations of states where one electron has been excited from an occupied HMO Ψ\Psi to an unoccupied HMO Ψ′\Psi^{\prime}. Now, though, the form factor involves taking linear combinations of the single-particle matrix elements and then squaring, reflecting the fact that the system can be treated with the full many-body states. Because all orbitals are simply spatial translations of the same 2pz orbital, the linearity of the Fourier transform means that there is only a single primary integral to compute, involving the momentum-space orbital

ϕ~2​pz​(𝐤)=Zeff7/2​a03/2π​kz​a0(k2​a02+(Zeff/2)2)3\widetilde{\phi}_{2p_{z}}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{Z_{\rm eff}^{7/2}a_{0}^{3/2}}{\pi}\frac{k_{z}a_{0}}{(k^{2}a_{0}^{2}+(Z_{\rm eff}/2)^{2})^{3}} (147)

weighted by phase factors and coefficients which can be taken from the literature and/or determined from symmetry considerations for a large number of organic scintillators. From there on, the formalism for computing the scattering rate is identical to atomic ionization, with the small modification that the continuous spectrum of ionized states is replaced by a sum over the discrete spectrum of bound states. The first limits on DM-electron scattering from 1.3 kg of organic scintillator EJ-301 (doped p-xylene) using a photomultiplier tube readout were set in 2019 [150], and are competitive with current constraints from low-mass semiconductor detectors in the few-MeV mass range for mχm_{\chi}, though many improvements on this setup are possible.

As can be seen from Eq. (147), the electrons in the 2pz orbitals break spherical symmetry, leading to an anisotropic form factor for transitions where these orbitals dominate. Define the scintillation transition form factors from the (many-body) ground state |ψG⟩|\psi_{G}\rangle to scintillation state |ψsi⟩|\psi_{s_{i}}\rangle, with energy Δ​Ei\Delta E_{i} with respect to the ground state, as

fi​(𝐪)=⟨ψsi|∑k=1NCei​𝐪⋅𝐫k|ψG⟩f_{i}(\mathbf{q})=\langle\psi_{s_{i}}|\sum_{k=1}^{N_{C}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{k}}|\psi_{G}\rangle (148)

where the sum runs over the kk delocalized electrons, equal to the number NCN_{C} of carbon atoms in the molecule. This notation differs somewhat from the atomic case since we are only indexing the transition by its energy, rather than labeling the initial and final states by individual orbitals, due to the fact that the electron-electron interactions in the molecule have caused these orbitals to mix. Using Eqs. (17) and (18) for the time-dependent rate, the rate for observing a scintillation photon is

R⁡(t)=ξ​Nmol​ρχmχ​σ¯eμχ​e2​∑i∫d3​𝐪4​π​g​(𝐪,Δ​Ei,t)​FDM2​(q)​|fi​(𝐪)|2,R(t)=\xi N_{\rm mol}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\sum_{i}\int\!\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{4\pi}g(\mathbf{q},\Delta E_{i};t)F_{\text{DM}}^{2}(q)|f_{i}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}, (149)

where NmolN_{\rm mol} is the number of molecules per unit detector mass, ξ\xi is a quantum efficiency factor representing the probability that the de-excitation of a scintillation state yields a photon which escapes the sample, and the sum runs over all transitions to singlet states. Some examples of form factors for the lowest s1s_{1} transition in t-stilbene (which can be grown as high-quality single crystals, preserving the directionality of the form factors) and the associated time-dependent rate for various DM masses are shown in Fig. 16. The anisotropy is clear, leading to a large modulation amplitude of ≃50%\simeq 50\% for mχ=2​MeVm_{\chi}=2\ {\rm MeV} for an orientation of the crystal axis with respect to the zz-axis given by β=90∘\beta=90^{\circ} (see Ref. [127] for details). The 4-fold symmetry of the form factor is due to the presence of 4 molecules in the unit cell with different orientations; the anisotropy would be even larger in a crystal with fewer independent molecular orientations.

Note that the form factor peaks at a typical scale q∗≃6​keVq^{*}\simeq 6\ {\rm keV}, of order the inverse carbon-carbon bond length, consistent with the arguments at the beginning of this section. Since the minimum-allowed qq in a scattering event is qmin=Δ​E/vq_{\rm min}=\Delta E/v, we can define an effective velocity scale

v∗≡Δ​Eq∗v^{*}\equiv\frac{\Delta E}{q^{*}} (150)

such that the peak of the form factor is accessible if v>v∗v>v^{*}. In t-stilbene, v∗≃200​km/sv^{*}\simeq 200\ {\rm km/s}, and the form factor peaks are accessible to the bulk of the DM velocity distribution in the SHM, a fortuitous coincidence given that v∗v^{*} and v0v_{0} are set by completely different physical mechanisms! As we will see below, this yields a total rate per unit mass for organic scintillators which is within a factor of a few of silicon. However, this same fact leads to a smaller ∼10%\sim 10\% daily modulation amplitude at large DM masses, due largely to structure of the secondary peaks in the form factor at q≃1.2​keVq\simeq 1.2\ {\rm keV} (comparable to the inverse size of the entire molecule). Indeed, daily modulation is mainly a threshold effect, occurring when form factor peaks are kinematically accessible for some values of 𝐪⋅𝐯\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{v} but not others, and thus depends sensitively on the high-velocity tail of the DM distribution. Thus, there is an inevitable trade-off between maximizing the total rate and maximizing the modulation amplitude, an effect also seen in the analogous daily modulation signal in phonons [107, 103, 112]. The enhanced statistical power of a modulating rate, even in the presence of a nonzero (but non-modulating) background rate, may be favorable over simply maximizing the total rate if zero-background operation is not feasible.

V.3 Solid-state excitation and collective modes

To probe dark matter with MeV mass or below, electronic excitation energies at the eV scale and below are required, necessitating the use of solid-state systems with the required low band gaps. Historically, much of the theoretical and experimental effort has focused on conventional semiconductor detectors – specifically silicon and germanium – as well as conventional superconductors like aluminum. Recently there has been a flourishing effort to identify new materials with particular properties which are well-suited to the kinematics of sub-GeV DM. We will survey these new candidate in materials in Sec. VIII.1, and focus here on a particular illustrative example, Dirac materials, which has a band structure suitable for semi-analytic calculations of the dynamic structure factor.

The first calculations of DM-electron scattering in silicon and germanium used either DFT band structures and wavefunctions [18, 155] or semi-analytic models based on hydrogenic or tight-binding orbitals [126, 43]. By the arguments at the beginning of this section, the typical momentum transfers probe electrons on length scales smaller than a single unit cell as long as the gap is 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}({\rm eV}) or larger, so both of these approaches are expected to give the correct order of magnitude for the total scattering rate, though there are important differences between the spectra at small and large recoil energies, as we will discuss shortly.

We first review the original DFT approach of Ref. [155], which amounts to the following procedure: start with Eq. (53), treat the initial and final states as Bloch states, and neglect the sum over all electrons in the operator by taking ∑kei​𝐪⋅𝐫k→ei​𝐪⋅𝐫\sum_{k}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{k}}\to e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}. First, using the Bloch wave parametrization of Eq. (38) and the Fourier expansion of the cell function (35), we may write the single-particle wavefunctions as

ψi​𝐤​(𝐫)=1V​∑𝐆ui​(𝐤+𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫\psi_{i\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}u_{i}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}} (151)

where ii is a band index, 𝐤\mathbf{k} is a crystal momentum, and 𝐆\mathbf{G} is a reciprocal lattice vector. The normalization of the wavefunction is enforced by ∑𝐆|ui​(𝐤+𝐆)|2=1\sum_{\mathbf{G}}|u_{i}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})|^{2}=1. The analogue to the atomic form factor is given by single-particle wavefunction overlaps [155]

|fi​𝐤→i′​𝐤′|2\displaystyle|f_{i\mathbf{k}\to i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}|^{2} =∑𝐆′(2​π)3​δ3​(𝐪−(𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆′))V​|∑𝐆ui′∗​(𝐤′+𝐆+𝐆′)​ui​(𝐤+𝐆)|2\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{q}-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}))}{V}\left|\sum_{\mathbf{G}}u^{*}_{i^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime})u_{i}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\right|^{2} (152)
≡∑𝐆′(2​π)3​δ3​(𝐪−(𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆′))V​|f[i​𝐤,i′​𝐤′,𝐆′]|2,\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{q}-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}))}{V}|f_{[i\mathbf{k},i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}]}|^{2}, (153)

where the delta function makes explicit that crystal momentum is conserved only up to a reciprocal lattice vector. Note that we will use ii to label valence bands and i′i^{\prime} to label conduction bands, assuming the target is at zero temperature. Similarly, summing over initial and final states and bands (including an explicit factor of 2 for spin degeneracy) and assuming an isotropic DM velocity distribution yields the analogue of the ionization form factor

|fcrystal​(q,ω)|2=2​π2α​me2​Ω​ω​∑i,i′∫BZΩ​d3​k(2​π)3​Ω​d3​k′(2​π)3​ω​δ​(ω−Ei′​𝐤′+Ei​𝐤)​∑𝐆′q​δ​(q−|𝐤′−𝐤+𝐆′|)​|f[i​𝐤,i′​𝐤′,𝐆′]|2|f_{\rm crystal}(q,\omega)|^{2}=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{\alpha m_{e}^{2}\Omega\,\omega}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}}\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{\Omega d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{\Omega d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\omega\delta(\omega-E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}+E_{i\mathbf{k}})\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}q\delta(q-|\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}|)|f_{[i\mathbf{k},i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}]}|^{2} (154)

referred to as the crystal form factor. Here, the integral is taken over the 1BZ and Ω\Omega is again the unit cell volume. By analogy to Eq. (140), the spectrum is

d​Rd​ln⁡ω=1Ω​ρT​ρχmχ​σ¯e​α×[me2μχ​e2​∫d​ln⁡q⁡(ωq​η​(vmin)​|FDM​(q)|2​|fcrystal​(q,ω)|2)].\frac{dR}{d\ln\omega}=\frac{1}{\Omega\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\overline{\sigma}_{e}\alpha\times\left[\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int d\,\ln q\,\left(\frac{\omega}{q}\eta(v_{\rm min})|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{\rm crystal}(q,\omega)|^{2}\right)\right]. (155)

Note that now ω\omega is total energy deposited, while in the atomic case we gave the differential rate with respect to the outgoing energy of the ionized electron, EerE_{\rm er}, which differs from the total deposited energy by the binding energy of the initial-state orbital. In Eq. (155), the factor in square brackets is a dimensionless 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) number when q∼p0q\sim p_{0} and ω∼𝒪⁡(5​eV)\omega\sim\mathcal{O}(5\ {\rm eV}), since ω/q≃10−3≃v\omega/q\simeq 10^{-3}\simeq v while η⁡(vmin)∼1/v\eta(v_{\rm min})\sim 1/v. For mχ=10​MeVm_{\chi}=10\ {\rm MeV} and σ¯e=10−37\overline{\sigma}_{e}=10^{-37} cm2 at the freeze-out cross section, this gives an expected rate of 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) events/min/kg, a sizable rate compared to WIMP experiments!

One limitation of the DFT approach is that it is computationally expensive to include high-momentum components of the wavefunctions, which are needed for scattering of heavier DM and to describe excitations of core or semi-core electrons. For instance, in germanium, the 3d electron shell generates an important contribution to the spectrum above about 30 eV [43]. The importance of including these components was emphasized in Ref. [156], which used the projector augmented wave (PAW) method for an “all-electron” reconstruction of the wavefunctions, but this treatment was still limited to DM masses below about 100 MeV. Recently, Ref. [129] extended the PAW approach and also included core electrons by a semi-analytic method similar to that of Refs. [126, 43]. In particular, Ref. [129] showed that the core electron wavefunctions are accurately modeled in a basis of Wannier orbitals

ψi​𝐤​(𝐫)=1N​∑i=1Nei​𝐤⋅𝐑i​ϕ​(𝐫−𝐑i)\psi_{i\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{i}}\phi(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{i}) (156)

where the sum runs over all lattice sites with positions 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i}. The Wannier functions ϕ\phi are typically taken to be linear combinations of atomic orbitals, similar to those used in Secs. V.1 and V.2. Since qmin≫|𝐑i−𝐑j|−1q_{\rm min}\gg|\mathbf{R}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{j}|^{-1} for the high-momentum transfers of interest, the sum is mostly incoherent and the crystal form factor can be approximated with an atomic form factor. The conclusion of Ref. [129] is that rates can be much larger for excitation energies ≳25\gtrsim 25 eV and that for Ge in particular, scattering of 3d electrons dominates for DM mass above 30 MeV and a heavy mediator, as shown in Fig. 17.

V.3.1 Dynamic structure factor for electron scattering

To make contact with the dynamic structure factor language of Sec. III.2, and to see the appearance of many-body effects, recall that we determined a general relationship between the dynamic structure factor and the dielectric function ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega), Eq. (58). We can see how the single-particle form factor Eq. (154) arises from Eq. (58) if we use a particular approximation for the dielectric function called the random phase approximation (RPA) [157]. Within RPA, we treat the medium as a degenerate gas of weakly-coupled quasiparticle excitations and use perturbation theory to compute the loop to absorb and emit single-electron excitations, yielding the Lindhard dielectric function,

ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)=1−4​π​αV​q2​∑𝐤,𝐤′,i,i′|⟨𝐤′,i′​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|​𝐤,i⟩|2​limη→0f0​(Ei′​𝐤′)−f0​(Ei​𝐤)Ei′​𝐤′−Ei​𝐤−ω−i​η,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)=1-\frac{4\pi\alpha}{Vq^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i,i^{\prime}}|\langle\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i^{\prime}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|\mathbf{k},i\rangle|^{2}\lim_{\eta\to 0}\frac{f^{0}(E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}})-f^{0}(E_{i\mathbf{k}})}{E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}-E_{i\mathbf{k}}-\omega-i\eta}, (157)

where |𝐤,i⟩|\mathbf{k},i\rangle denotes Bloch states. This approximation to the dielectric function is essentially computing the polarization in a noninteracting gas.2020 20 A potentially confusing piece of nomenclature, standard in the condensed matter literature, is that “noninteracting” refers to the fact that the electrons are treated as not directly interacting particle-by-particle when calculating the leading-order response function to an external probe. However, one obtains an approximation to the dielectric function of an interacting gas by self-consistently treating each individual electron as feeling the average potential accounting for all the other electrons [81]. In field theory language, the ground state of the system is corrected by the photon vacuum polarization diagram, which is calculated by neglecting electron-electron interactions. Note that ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega) acquires an imaginary part when the denominator becomes singular:

Im​ϵ​(𝐪,ω)=4​π2​αV​q2​∑𝐤,𝐤′,i,i′|⟨𝐤′,i′​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|​𝐤,i⟩|2​δ​(ω+Ei​𝐤−Ei′​𝐤′),{\rm Im}\,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{4\pi^{2}\alpha}{Vq^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i,i^{\prime}}|\langle\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i^{\prime}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|\mathbf{k},i\rangle|^{2}\delta(\omega+E_{i\mathbf{k}}-E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}), (158)

using the Dirac identity Im⁡(limη→01x−i​η)=π​δ​(x){\rm Im}(\lim_{\eta\to 0}\frac{1}{x-i\eta})=\pi\delta(x). Then the dynamic structure factor can be written as

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=q22​π​α​Im​(−1ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω))=2​πV​|ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|2​∑𝐤,𝐤′,i,i′|⟨𝐤′,i′​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|​𝐤,i⟩|2​δ​(ω+Ei​𝐤−Ei′​𝐤′).S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{q^{2}}{2\pi\alpha}{\rm Im}\left(-\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)}\right)=\frac{2\pi}{V|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i,i^{\prime}}|\langle\mathbf{k}^{\prime},i^{\prime}|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|\mathbf{k},i\rangle|^{2}\delta(\omega+E_{i\mathbf{k}}-E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}). (159)

S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) has the expected form if we were to start with Eq. (53) and treat the initial and final states as Bloch states, which led to the rate in Eqs. (154-155), but here an additional factor of 1/|ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|21/|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2} appears. The difference arises from the fact that the true initial and final states are many-body states, and the actual result in terms of single-particle states must account for the total response of the medium, which screens any external perturbation by ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega). In other words, the factor of 1/|ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|21/|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2} accounts for in-medium screening effects and is equivalent to resumming an infinite series of insertions of the polarization loop, where we see explicitly that the structure factor includes terms to all orders in α\alpha.2121 21 These “in-medium” effects may be though of as corrections to the propagator of the mediator for DM-electron interactions [158], or qq-dependent modifications to the DM-electron coupling [19], but here we include them directly in the dynamic structure factor. We can also write S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) explicitly in terms of the same wavefunction overlaps as before using Eq. (151) for the initial and final states [128]:

S⁡(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle S(\mathbf{q},\omega) =2​π|ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|2​∑i,i′∫2​d3​𝐤(2​π)3​d3​𝐤′(2​π)3​|f[i​𝐤,i′​𝐤′,𝐆′]|2​∑𝐆(2​π)3​δ3​(𝐪+𝐤−𝐤′−𝐆)​δ​(ω−Ei′​𝐤′+Ei​𝐤)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2}}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}}\int\frac{2d^{3}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}|f_{[i\mathbf{k},i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}]}|^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{G})\delta(\omega-E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}+E_{i\mathbf{k}}) (160)
=8​π2​α2​me2q5​Ω​|fcrystal​(q,ω)|2|ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|2,\displaystyle=\frac{8\pi^{2}\alpha^{2}m_{e}^{2}}{q^{5}\Omega}\frac{|f_{\rm crystal}(q,\omega)|^{2}}{|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2}}, (161)

where the second line is obtained by comparing with Eq. (154). For typical momentum transfers q≫qcohq\gg q_{\rm coh}, |ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|2≈1|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2}\approx 1 and screening will lead to O⁡(1)O(1) effects, though this is needed to obtain precise predictions of the scattering rate beyond an order-of-magnitude estimate.

While the interpretation of the dielectric function in terms of single-particle Bloch states is only true within RPA, the relationship between the dielectric function and the scattering rate is more general. For spin-independent DM-electron scattering, which may arise from exchange of a scalar or vector mediator, the transition rate for a fixed DM velocity 𝐯\mathbf{v} is [131, 128]

Γ⁡(𝐯)=π​σ¯eμχ​e2​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​|FDM​(q)|2​[q22​π​α​Im​(−1ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω𝐪))],\Gamma(\mathbf{v})=\frac{\pi\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}\,\left[\frac{q^{2}}{2\pi\alpha}\,{\rm Im}\left(-\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega_{\mathbf{q}})}\right)\right], (162)

which is proportional to the ELF 𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega) (Eq. (61)) and the DM-electron scattering potential V⁡(q)V(q) (or equivalently, the DM form factor FDM​(q)F_{\rm DM}(q)).2222 22 See Refs. [159, 160] for a discussion of interactions beyond spin-independent couplings to electron density, performed in the single-particle Bloch wave basis. See also a dedicated study of magnon excitation by spin-dependent scattering in Ref. [161]. Assuming an isotropic velocity dispersion, the spectrum per unit mass is

d​Rd​ω=1ρT​ρχmχ​π​σ¯eμχ​e2​∫d​q​q3(2​π)3​α​|FDM​(q)|2​η​(vmin​(q,ω))​𝒲​(q,ω).\frac{dR}{d\omega}=\frac{1}{\rho_{T}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\bar{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{dq\,q^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}\alpha}\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}\eta\bigl(v_{\mathrm{min}}(q,\omega)\bigr)\mathcal{W}(q,\omega). (163)

Using Eq. (161) for the Lindhard dielectric, we see that Eq. (163) exactly matches previous results (155) using DFT wavefunctions except for the factor of 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2}. This makes it clear that the objects of interest are not the single-particle wavefunctions themselves, but rather the particular combination which appears in the dynamic structure factor.

The advantages of the dielectric function formalism for spin-independent scattering are that there are many simple analytic models and detailed condensed matter calculations for ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega), and that for many common (and some less-common) materials, ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega) has been directly measured. The free-electron gas (FEG) dielectric function (somewhat confusingly, also commonly referred to as the Lindhard function) is a particularly useful analytic model which captures important scales in the problem. In this model, the electrons are assumed to fill up an isotropic Fermi sphere with no band gap or lattice structure, which gives [162]

ϵFEG(𝐪,ω)=1+limη→03​ωp2q2​vF2{12+kF4​q(1−(q2​kF−ω+i​ηq​vF)2)Log(q2​kF−ω+i​ηq​vF+1q2​kF−ω+i​ηq​vF−1)+kF4​q(1−(q2​kF+ω+i​ηq​vF)2)Log(q2​kF+ω+i​ηq​vF+1q2​kF+ω+i​ηq​vF−1)}.\epsilon_{\rm FEG}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=1+\lim_{\eta\to 0}\frac{3\omega_{p}^{2}}{q^{2}v_{F}^{2}}\Biggl\{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{k_{F}}{4q}\left(1-\left(\frac{q}{2k_{F}}-\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}\right)^{2}\right)\operatorname{Log}\left(\frac{\frac{q}{2k_{F}}-\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}+1}{\frac{q}{2k_{F}}-\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}-1}\right)\\ +\frac{k_{F}}{4q}\left(1-\left(\frac{q}{2k_{F}}+\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}\right)^{2}\right)\operatorname{Log}\left(\frac{\frac{q}{2k_{F}}+\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}+1}{\frac{q}{2k_{F}}+\frac{\omega+i\eta}{qv_{F}}-1}\right)\Biggr\}. (164)

The free parameter in this model is the electron density nen_{e}, in terms of which we have

kF=(3​π2​ne)1/3,vF=kFme,ωp=4​π​α​neme.k_{F}=(3\pi^{2}n_{e})^{1/3},\qquad v_{F}=\frac{k_{F}}{m_{e}},\qquad\omega_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi\alpha n_{e}}{m_{e}}}. (165)

Typical values for the FEG model parameters are

kF≃5​keV≃p0,vF≃10−2,ωp≃15​eV.k_{F}\simeq 5\ {\rm keV}\simeq p_{0},\qquad v_{F}\simeq 10^{-2},\qquad\omega_{p}\simeq 15\ {\rm eV}. (166)

In general, the ELF in an isotropic medium must satisfy two important consistency conditions, arising from its origin as a causal correlation function:

𝒲⁡(𝐪,−ω)=−𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω),∫0∞d​ω​ω​𝒲​(𝐪,ω)=π2​ωp2.\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},-\omega)=-\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega),\qquad\int_{0}^{\infty}d\omega\,\omega\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{\pi}{2}\omega_{p}^{2}. (167)

The integral constraint is known as the f-sum rule, and both are satisfied by the FEG dielectric function. One limitation of the FEG is that it doesn’t account for finite electron damping time or the plasmon width; this can be accounted for in the Mermin dielectric function with damping parameter Γp\Gamma_{p} [163]:

ϵMermin​(𝐪,ω)≡1+(1+i​Γp/ω)​[ϵFEG​(𝐪,ω+i​Γp)−1]1+i​Γp/ω⁡[ϵFEG​(𝐪,ω+i​Γp)−1ϵFEG​(𝐪,0)−1]\epsilon_{\rm Mermin}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv 1+\frac{(1+i\Gamma_{p}/\omega)\left[\epsilon_{\rm FEG}(\mathbf{q},\omega+i\Gamma_{p})-1\right]}{1+i\Gamma_{p}/\omega\left[\frac{\epsilon_{\rm FEG}(\mathbf{q},\omega+i\Gamma_{p})-1}{\epsilon_{\rm FEG}(\mathbf{q},0)-1}\right]} (168)

In particular, one can also take a linear combination of Mermin models with different nen_{e}, fitted to experimental measurements of energy loss or dielectric functions and appropriately weighted to satisfy the ff-sum rule [84, 85, 86]. This is called the Mermin oscillator model.

In Fig. 18, we show the dynamic structure factor calculated with the FEG dielectric function in the limit Γp→0\Gamma_{p}\to 0 and with a DFT calculation for Si from Ref. [128]. In both cases, there is a strong resonance at low qq and ω≃10−20\omega\simeq 10-20 eV associated with the plasmon excitation, with is infinitely narrow in the left panel but has a finite width of a few eV in the right panel. At high qq, there is broad support for the dynamic structure factor, interpreted here as electron-hole excitations, which are peaked about the free-electron dispersion q2/(2​me)q^{2}/(2m_{e}). An important difference between the two structure factors is that the dynamic structure factor goes to zero as ω\omega approaches the band gap of the material. However, for ω\omega somewhat above the band gap and q>qminq>q_{\rm min} for DM scattering, we see that the two structure factors are qualitatively quite similar. Indeed, as shown in Refs. [131, 113], the FEG model describes the DM-electron spectrum for ω∈[5,15]​eV\omega\in[5,15]\ {\rm eV} in Si and Ge semiconductors quite well. For higher energies, it is also expected that the FEG model fails to capture the localized core electrons and the associated high-momentum tails. This can be improved on by generalizing the FEG ELF to the Mermin oscillator model fitted to experimental data, which gives good agreement with DFT calculations at higher energies and momenta as well, see Refs. [128, 113]. Note there is also good agreement among independent DFT calculations accounting for screening effects [128, 164, 129].

The upshot of this discussion is that the FEG dielectric function provides a useful analytic model to understand the dynamic structure factor in conventional semiconductors and metals, and we can use it here to explore the features and general behavior of the structure factor in several limits:

  • •

    For q≫kFq\gg k_{F}, the FEG ELF is maximized at ω≃q2​vF2​kF\omega\simeq\frac{q^{2}v_{F}}{2k_{F}}. For vF=kF/mev_{F}=k_{F}/m_{e}, this relation is simply the dispersion for elastic scattering, ω=q2/(2​me)\omega=q^{2}/(2m_{e}), reflecting the fact that electrons are mostly independent particles at large qq. The width of the peak is quite broad, since the Fermi velocity of electrons at the Fermi surface is sizeable, but at q≫kFq\gg k_{F}, the scattering rate converges to that of free-electron scattering.

  • •

    For lower q≲kFq\lesssim k_{F}, screening and many-body effects effects start to play an important role. Taking q≪kFq\ll k_{F} and ω≪q​vF\omega\ll qv_{F}, we have

    ϵFEG​(𝐪,ω)≈λTF22​q2+i​3​π​ωp2​ω2​q3​vF3(q≪kF,ω≪q​vF)\epsilon_{\rm FEG}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{\lambda_{\rm TF}^{2}}{2q^{2}}+i\frac{3\pi\omega_{p}^{2}\omega}{2q^{3}v_{F}^{3}}\qquad(q\ll k_{F},\ \omega\ll qv_{F}) (169)

    where λTF=ωp​vF/3\lambda_{\rm TF}=\omega_{p}v_{F}/\sqrt{3} is the inverse Thomas-Fermi screening length. The fact that |ϵ|2≫1|\epsilon|^{2}\gg 1 in the low-momentum regime is a manifestation of long-range charge screening. For typical values of the FEG parameters, Re​ϵ≫Im​ϵ{\rm Re}\,\epsilon\gg{\rm Im}\,\epsilon, so we may approximate the ELF as

    𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)≈Im​ϵ​(𝐪,ω)(Re​ϵ​(𝐪,ω))2≈6​π​ωp2λTF4​vF3​ω​q(q≪kF,ω≪q​vF)\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{{\rm Im}\,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)}{({\rm Re}\,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega))^{2}}\approx\frac{6\pi\omega_{p}^{2}}{\lambda_{\rm TF}^{4}v_{F}^{3}}\omega q\qquad(q\ll k_{F},\ \omega\ll qv_{F}) (170)

    which vanishes as q→0q\to 0.

  • •

    At small q<kFq<k_{F} but larger energy ω≳q​vF\omega\gtrsim qv_{F}, collective modes emerge from the ELF. The FEG model gives rise to poles:

    limq→0𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)=π​ωp2​(δ⁡(ω−ωp)−δ⁡(ω+ωp))\lim_{q\to 0}\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{\pi\omega_{p}}{2}\left(\delta(\omega-\omega_{p})-\delta(\omega+\omega_{p})\right) (171)

    which describes a plasmon mode of energy ωp\omega_{p} where all of the valence electrons in the material are oscillating in phase at the classical plasma frequency. At finite qq, the plasmon pole has a dispersion relation given by ω2≈ωp2+3​q2​vF2/5\omega^{2}\approx\omega_{p}^{2}+3q^{2}v_{F}^{2}/5 and extends up to a cutoff momentum qc≃ωp/vFq_{c}\simeq\omega_{p}/v_{F}, beyond which Landau damping occurs and the plasmon can efficiently decay into electron-hole pairs. In a realistic material, various decay paths for the plasmon are also available for q<qcq<q_{c}, so that we should use the Mermin dielectric function, Eq. (168), with finite Γp\Gamma_{p} to represent the plasmon width, which yields at q=0q=0

    limq→0𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)=ωp2​ω​Γp(ωp2−ω2)2+ω2​Γp2.\lim_{q\to 0}\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{\omega_{p}^{2}\omega\Gamma_{p}}{(\omega_{p}^{2}-\omega^{2})^{2}+\omega^{2}\Gamma_{p}^{2}}. (172)

    Using the relation between the dynamic structure factor and the ELF, Eq. (58), we see that S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) scales as q2​ωq^{2}\omega at small qq and ω\omega as claimed in Eq. (59). This Breit-Wigner lineshape is the same as what would be obtained from treating the valence electrons as a damped harmonic oscillator (the Fröhlich model). The measured plasmon lineshapes in both semiconductors like Si and Ge [83] and metals like Al [165, 166] are extremely close to this simple form.

From the identification of the peaks of the ELF (and thus dynamic structure factor), we learn that conventional metals and semiconductors are not optimal in terms of matching the DM scattering phase space, which requires ω<q​vmax\omega<qv_{\rm max}. At q>kFq>k_{F}, the peak at ω∼q2/(2​me)\omega\sim q^{2}/(2m_{e}) is not accessible, since in this regime ω≳q​kF/me∼q​α\omega\gtrsim qk_{F}/m_{e}\sim q\alpha. At low q<kFq<k_{F}, most of the weight in the ELF is carried by the plasmon which is located at ω>q​vF\omega>qv_{F}. However, the DM velocity is typically much slower than the Fermi velocity in conventional materials, so that the DM cannot access the plasmon.2323 23 A fast subcomponent of DM, arising for example from supernova remnants [167], may excite the plasmon directly [168]. DM-nucleus scattering can also excite the plasmon through a 2→32\to 3 process [168, 169], as will be discussed in more detail in Sec. VI. Since the integrated weight of the ELF is constrained by the ff-sum rule, it is in this sense that DM-electron scattering in conventional materials is “inefficient” as was the case for multi-phonon excitations in superfluid helium. However, semiconductors are still better than a typical atomic target as in Fig. 13, due to the lower gaps. Projections in terms of the DM-electron cross section are shown in Fig. 12 for example semiconductors of Si and Ge.

V.3.2 Sub-MeV DM scattering

The small-qq regime is especially important for sub-MeV DM, which carries maximum momentum pχ<1​keV≪kFp_{\chi}<1\ {\rm keV}\ll k_{F}. This regime is accessible in superconductors, which have a gap Δ≲𝒪⁡(meV)\Delta\lesssim\ \mathcal{O}({\rm meV}) and hence qq can be as small as 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}({\rm eV}) for DM scattering. Ref. [170] first pointed out the suitability of superconductors for sub-MeV DM, using the FEG model to compute scattering for ω≫Δ\omega\gg\Delta. Ref. [158] noted the reach is suppressed for a dark photon mediator because of screening effects; recently, Refs. [131, 128], using the dielectric formalism, clarified that screening is present for all scalar and vector mediators (not just dark photons), and furthermore that the reach is considerably better than previously estimated because [158] effectively used a loss function which did not satisfy the causality property due to an incorrect choice of branch cut.2424 24 As noted in [131], there may also be additional contributions to the ELF from the plasmon tail, which would further improve the reach, but dedicated measurements are required in the small-qq regime to confirm the presence of the tail; Ref. [166] shows the tail in aluminum extending down to 0.1 eV. The projected reach for different energy thresholds is given by the Al lines in Fig. 12.

The screening effects in a superconductor can be traced back to the behavior of the ELF in the low qq limit, Eq. (170). This behavior gets cutoff in a semiconductor, since in the limit of low q,ωq,\omega we should reproduce the static dielectric function which is typically 𝒪⁡(1−10)\mathcal{O}(1-10). We can see the finite behavior of the dielectric function in this case from the Lindhard formula (157). In the limit q→0q\to 0, the squared matrix element must then vanish like q2q^{2} as q→0q\to 0, since we are considering orthogonal states. At the same time, in a semiconductor or insulator, the Fermi level lies in the gap and the lowest-energy excitations are interband transitions between bands, so that energy differences Ei′​𝐤′−Ei​𝐤=Ei′​𝐤+𝐪−Ei​𝐤E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}-E_{i\mathbf{k}}=E_{i^{\prime}\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}-E_{i\mathbf{k}} should be approximately independent of qq. The q2q^{2} from the matrix overlap then cancels the Coulomb prefactor and yields a constant ϵ\epsilon. An alternate parameterization of the dielectric function for semiconductors at low qq can be found in Ref. [171]. Thus, large screening effects at small qq are absent in materials with a Fermi level lying between the valence and conduction bands, which motivates considering narrow-gap semiconductors as targets to enhance the sub-MeV DM scattering rate.

An example of such a narrow-gap semiconductor is a gapped Dirac material, so named because the valence and conduction bands have dispersion relations which approximate the relativistic dispersion, E±​(𝐤)=vF2​𝐤2+Δ2E_{\pm}(\mathbf{k})=\sqrt{v_{F}^{2}\mathbf{k}^{2}+\Delta^{2}}, with the gap 2​Δ2\Delta playing the role of (twice) the relativistic particle mass. The point in the BZ with 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0 is known as the Dirac point. Ref. [172] first determined the scattering rate in Dirac materials by computing the single-particle matrix elements ⟨𝐤+𝐪;+|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫|𝐤;−⟩\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q};+|e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}|\mathbf{k};-\rangle between the uppermost valence (−-) and lowest conduction (++) bands, imposing a momentum cutoff at |𝐤|=Λ|\mathbf{k}|=\Lambda where the dispersion deviates from the relativistic form, and dividing by |ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)|2|\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)|^{2} to account for screening. This is equivalent to simply computing the ELF directly, which we will do here as it is somewhat more transparent. Assuming that the −- and ++ bands are the only bands which contribute to the dielectric function, ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega) may be computed in exact analogy with the 1-loop vacuum polarization in quantum electrodynamics, with appropriate factors of vFv_{F} instead of cc. The momentum cutoff corresponds to the familiar UV cutoff in 1-loop diagrams, and the result is

ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)=1+\displaystyle\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)=1+ e24​π2​vF​∫01d​x​{x⁡(1−x)​ln⁡|(2​vF​Λ)2Δ2−x⁡(1−x)​(ω2−vF2​𝐪2)|}\displaystyle\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi^{2}v_{F}}\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\left\{x(1-x)\ln\left|\frac{(2v_{F}\Lambda)^{2}}{\Delta^{2}-x(1-x)(\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}\mathbf{q}^{2})}\right|\right\}
+i​e224​π​κ​vF​1−4​Δ2ω2−vF2​𝐪2​(1+2​Δ2ω2−vF2​𝐪2)​Θ​(ω2−vF2​𝐪2−4​Δ2).\displaystyle+i\frac{e^{2}}{24\pi\kappa v_{F}}\sqrt{1-\frac{4\Delta^{2}}{\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}\mathbf{q}^{2}}}\left(1+\frac{2\Delta^{2}}{\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}\mathbf{q}^{2}}\right)\Theta(\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}\mathbf{q}^{2}-4\Delta^{2}). (173)

However, as noted in Ref. [130], this calculation for the real part of ϵ\epsilon is unreliable because DFT calculations show that Re​ϵ{\rm Re}\,\epsilon receives contributions from the entire BZ, not just the region around the Dirac point with |𝐤|<Λ|\mathbf{k}|<\Lambda. Thus, we may approximate Re​ϵ​(𝐪,ω)≈ϵ⁡(𝟎,0)=κ≫1{\rm Re}\,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\epsilon(\mathbf{0},0)=\kappa\gg 1 as a background static dielectric constant which should be measured or determined from DFT. The imaginary part is unaffected by this complication, so assuming Im​ϵ≪κ{\rm Im}\,\epsilon\ll\kappa (which is in fact required for the perturbation theory calculation we used to determine ϵ\epsilon) we may compute the ELF as [131]

𝒲⁡(𝐪,ω)≈Im​ϵ​(𝐪,ω)κ2=e212​κ2​π​vF​1−4​Δ2ω2−vF2​q2​(1+2​Δ2ω2−vF2​q2)​Θ​(ω2−vF2​q2−4​Δ2)​Θ​(ωmax−ω)\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\approx\frac{{\rm Im}\,\epsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)}{\kappa^{2}}=\frac{e^{2}}{12\kappa^{2}\pi v_{F}}\sqrt{1-\frac{4\Delta^{2}}{\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}q^{2}}}\left(1+\frac{2\Delta^{2}}{\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}q^{2}}\right)\Theta(\omega^{2}-v_{F}^{2}q^{2}-4\Delta^{2})\Theta(\omega_{\mathrm{max}}-\omega) (174)

where we have replaced the momentum cutoff Λ\Lambda with an energy cutoff ωmax\omega_{\rm max}. In contrast to the FEG single-particle ELF (170), the Dirac ELF is unsuppressed by powers of qq and can thus lead to a larger scattering rate for small DM masses. In addition, scattering is forbidden for v<vFv<v_{F}, a peculiarity of the kinematics of linear dispersion. The projected reach for an example Dirac material of ZrTe5 is shown in Fig. 12. Dirac materials may also feature anisotropic dispersion relations, with parametrically different Fermi velocities vF,x,vF,y,vF,zv_{F,x},v_{F,y},v_{F,z} along different crystal axes, which allows for a large 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) daily modulation signal for sub-MeV DM [173, 130] (due partly to the requirement v>vFv>v_{F}), greatly improving the detection prospects if such a detector can be realized in the laboratory. Finally, we note that plasmons are also expected to exist in Dirac materials [174, 175, 176]; indeed, the ELF in Eq. (174) does not satisfy the ff-sum rule and therefore cannot represent the entire excitation spectrum because it only contains single-particle contributions. The effect of these contributions to the ELF on the DM-electron scattering rate remains to be fully evaluated.

VI The Migdal Effect

The main narrative emphasized the dynamic structure factor including only phonon excitations (Sec. IV) or only electronic excitations (Sec. IV). This is a good leading approximation, but there are regimes of phase space or situations where it is valuable to consider a mixed response in a dynamic structure factor. For instance, for DM-electron scattering below the gap, phonon modes are the only available excitations, and thus DM-electron scattering may lead to phonon production [107, 19]. At energies just above the band gap, the response function may be dominated by simultaneous production of an electron and phonon. This can be thought of as a 2→32\to 3 process, where an off-shell electron emits a phonon; in particular, it is distinct from possible subsequent interactions of the electron in the material, which may scatter off other electrons to produce phonons. This 2→32\to 3 process is known to be important in the limit of zero momentum transfer for indirect gap semiconductors, since the emission of phonon allows for conservation of crystal momentum. However, the energy of the phonon would generally be much smaller than that of the electronic excitation itself.

For DM-nucleus interactions, a similar 2→32\to 3 process is possible, with a nuclear recoil and electronic excitation being produced simultaneously. In this case, the possibility of a mixed electronic and nuclear response provides a more interesting prospect for experimental detection, since the electronic excitation could have comparable energy to the energy in phonons or nuclear recoil. Furthermore, at the present time the detection thresholds for electronic excitations are also much lower than for nuclear recoils (see Sec. VII), which means that it is possible to indirectly observe nuclear recoils of much lower mass DM with electronic detection approaches. This idea of producing a charge excitation from a nuclear interaction was originally studied and proposed in the context of atomic targets, where it is known as the Migdal effect [177, 178, 179]. Historically, it played a role in explaining observations of radioactive decays of heavy elements, which cause the sudden recoil of the nucleus [180, 181, 182, 183]. Discussions of the Migdal effect in DM-nucleus collisions first appeared in Refs. [184, 185], but it is only in recent years that interest has revived due to the interest in sub-GeV dark matter and the attainment of lower electronic thresholds [142]. The majority of theoretical studies have treated the target material as consisting of individual atomic targets [142, 186, 187, 188, 189, 190, 191, 192], similar to the original derivation by Migdal, while recently the effect has also been generalized to condensed matter targets [169, 99, 193].
